18534 Urgent Debates Declined 17 Jun 2014
Hon John Banks—Resignation as Member of Parliament

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received letters from the Rt Hon Winston Peters and the Hon
David Cunliffe seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the decision of the
Auckland High Court in relation to charges that the Hon John Banks filed a false
electoral return, his subsequent resignation, and its implications for confidence in the
Government. For there to be an urgent debate there must be a particular case of recent
occurrence that involves administrative or ministerial responsibility of the Government
that requires the urgent attention of the House. An urgent debate is a way of holding the
Government to account for an action for which it is responsible. There must be distinct
ministerial responsibility for the particular case for which the debate is sought.
There is no ministerial responsibility for the decision of the High Court or the
resignation of a member. Furthermore, an urgent debate is not an appropriate means of
exploring the question of confidence. The House procedures provide regular
opportunities to test the confidence in a Government. I understand the Government has
today lodged a notice of motion seeking to set aside a by -election in the seat of Epsom,
and that this is likely to be debated this week. This will provide the opportunity to
discuss the issues surrounding the resignation of the Hon John Banks. The applications
are therefore declined.

sections.heading: Debate On Crown Entities, Public Organisations, And State

items.text: In Committee

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: The debate on the performance of
Crown entities, public organisations, and State enterprises is a series of debates on
individual financial reviews of Crown entities, public organisations, and State
enterprises as reported by select committees. A total of 3 hours is allocated for the
debate. The debates on the individual financial reviews should be relevant to their
performance in their 2012 -13 financial year and their current operations. A member
may have no more than two calls on each financial review. The compendium of the
financial reviews available for debate is available on the Table. Reports on the entities
yet to be reported cannot be debated. I understand that m embers have indicated the
Crown entities, public organisations, and State enterprises they wish to debate. The first
entity I understand members wish to debate is the New Zealand Tourism Board.
New Zealand Tourism Board

items.speaker: Dr RUSSEL NORMAN
items.text: I rise to speak on the New Zealand
Tourism Board because I wish to discuss some of the challenges and headwinds that
Tourism New Zealand and the New Zealand tourism industry face as a r esult of this
Government.
As we know, the tourism industry is built on the “100% Pure New Zealand” brand.
The founding asset of the New Zealand tourism industry—and, of course, Tourism New
Zealand is an attempt to support that industry —is the natural envir onment of New
Zealand. In particular, it is the clean rivers of New Zealand. That natural environment is
under attack by this Government. Time after time, this Government has attacked the
founding asset of the New Zealand tourism industry —an industry built  on “100% Pure
New Zealand”. For example, we now have the problem where more than two -thirds of
our rivers are so polluted that they are unsafe for swimming. This is a major challenge
to the New Zealand tourism industry —an industry worth at least $6 billio n in exports
every year. The current Government has proposed new rules that would allow our rivers
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18535
to be even more polluted—so polluted they would not be safe to swim in; they would be
safe only to wade in.
What the Government is saying to the tourism indu stry is that it intends to pollute
New Zealand rivers to the level where you would be able to walk in them and put your
feet in them, but if you put your head under the water, then you would get sick and ill.
That is the standard that is being proposed by this Government, and that is one of the
problems that the tourism industry has to face. On top of that, the Government is
proposing to subsidise irrigation schemes to the tune of $400 million a year. We all
know that the major driver of the decline in wate r quality in New Zealand is the
intensive dairy sector. The Government is proposing to subsidise more intensive
agriculture, which will result in more polluted rivers. This is a challenge that the
tourism sector has to face. On the one hand, we know that o ur natural environment is
the founding asset of this sector. On the other hand, we have a Government that is out to
destroy that asset. It is out to destroy the goose that lays the golden egg, which is, of
course, the natural environment.
Let us talk about  the Environment Canterbury region. The elected councillors of
Environment Canterbury were removed from there by this Government because they
tried to protect rivers and lakes. For that reason, they had to be removed by the
Government. We know that the wat er is so polluted now in Canterbury the medical
officer of health has issued warnings that if you drink the water from your home bore,
then it could kill your babies—a thing called blue baby syndrome. The water now in the
ground water of Canterbury is so p olluted that the medical officer of health has issued
warnings that people should not give that water to their children in baby bottles. We
now have the situation where water is so polluted. This is a major threat to one of New
Zealand’s most important export sectors.
The most dangerous threat facing Tourism New Zealand right now is the National
Party. The National Party’s constant attacks on the natural environment will destroy the
long-term future of our tourism industry. A recent Environment Canterbury r eport has
identified that people with their own wells are at increased risk of campylobacter,
salmonella, cryptosporidium, and gastroenteritis in areas of dairy and major irrigation
schemes. So the Government is subsidising the very schemes that are destro ying water
quality and rivers and lakes across our country and, in the process, fundamentally
undermining and destroying the natural asset on which the entire tourism export sector
relies. One of New Zealand’s most important export industries, internationa l tourism, is
under attack by this Government as it consistently and constantly attacks rivers and
lakes across the country and subsidises their pollution.
If we do not change direction, we will not just have two -thirds of our rivers so
polluted that they are unsafe for swimming, we will have all of them. The Government
has proposed a new water quality standard that would mean that our rivers could be
more polluted than the Yangtze River in China, in terms of its nitrate pollution. That is
the standard that  the Government has recently issued in terms of water quality. If you
ever look at any of Tourism New Zealand’s documents, you will find that they are full
of pictures of our rivers and lakes as key attractions —key attractions for international
visitors. Yet this Government is doing everything it possibly can to pollute those rivers
and lakes. Right across the country, our rivers and lakes are highly polluted. Some of
them are so dangerous that if you swim in them you will get sick. They had to close
Lake Horowhenua because if you fell into the lake you could get liver damage. Time
after time after time our rivers and lakes are under attack from this Government.
Report noted.
18536 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
Reserve Bank of New Zealand

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: I rise to take a call in this
debate. I want to reflect on the mandate of the Reserve Bank, and why, in the view of
the Labour Party, we should as a Parliament update it to cater for the challen ges of
today. New Zealand has not had a current account surplus for 40 years. For 40 years we
have run a current account deficit.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Ha, ha!

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Whenever I say that, for some reason Mr Joyc e finds it
funny. He seems to think that getting back to about minus 3 percent of GDP as a current
account deficit is the best that it can ever get. It is the best that it will ever get under the
National Government because on these big calls National is a lways a follower; it is
never a leader. It was not a National Government that introduced the Reserve Bank of
New Zealand Act in the first place. It was not a National Government that introduced
the Cullen fund. National members opposed it —in fact, they cal led it a dog —but now
they say it is good. It was not a National Government that introduced KiwiSaver.
These long-term changes that make New Zealand a better place are generally brought
about by the Labour Party. The last time New Zealand had a current acc ount deficit we
had terms of trade that were good. But do you know what? They were not quite as good
as the terms of trade that we have just had. So in comparison with 40 years ago, when
we had terms of trade this good, New Zealand had a 2 percent current account surplus,
and we still have a deficit that is around 3 percent. It might get a wee bit under 3 percent
by the time it starts going out again, but then it is going to go back out to over 3 percent.
Every year that New Zealand has a current account d eficit it plugs the gap in one of
two ways, and generally a combination of both. It either borrows more money from
overseas lenders or it sells assets that were previously New Zealand - owned to overseas
owners. As a consequence, the burden on New Zealand’ s economy to pay interest or
dividend flows to those overseas lenders and owners grows every year.
Of course the control of inflation is important. Prior to our announcements there was
concern amongst some of the bank economists and academic economists that we were
going to lose that grounding—the target to control inflation. But we have not done that.
We have not done that.

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: No, that won’t change.

items.speaker: Hon DAVID PARKER
items.text: Mr Joyce chortles away there on the other side, but he is a
man of so little vision that he does not get the subtlety of any policy. He thinks the way
to go about policy is to employ more than 50 spin doctors at the Ministry of Business,
Innovation and Employment. That is his view of policy. The reality is that we can cause
the Reserve Bank to approach monetary policy in a way that best achieves external
balance over the cycle, and so that is what we have said it should do. If we do that, we
will also get the Reserve Bank encouraging better policy outcomes from the
Government.
We know that the reason interest rates are going up at the moment is that we have got
enormous house price inflation in Auckland at a time when general price inflation is
low. The fa ilure of Government policy around housing is responsible for those interest
rates going up higher than they would otherwise need to go. Part of that imbalance in
the economy is caused by biases in our tax system —notably, the absence of a capital
gains tax taxing speculative property purchases.
The National Party rattles on that we have already got a capital gains tax. That is not
true. We do tax as income some traders in property, but the vast majority of investors in
property who buy a property and then s ell it at a profit do not pay any tax on their
economic gains. The IMF, the OECD, Treasury, and the Reserve Bank all agree that
these cause imbalances. One of the reasons why the Government gets away with not
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18537
doing anything to address this —which is plainly in the interests of the economy even if
it is not in the interests of the minority of New Zealanders for whom this National
Government plainly governs and whose interests it prefers —is that the Reserve Bank is
never, under its current mandate, really stro ngly incentivised to say “Well, look, if you
don’t introduce a capital gains tax, we are going to have to push up interest rates.”
That is effectively the trade-off that we have in New Zealand at the moment, and yet
that is not exposed under current setti ngs. So the changes that we propose to monetary
policy would be one of the ways that New Zealand could keep its interest rates lower for
longer. We have interest rates that throughout the economic cycle are higher than those
of other countries. I am not ta lking about the variation within an economic cycle, the
timing of which will be different in New Zealand compared with overseas countries; I
am talking about overall New Zealand interest rates being about 1.5 to 2 percent higher
than they are in Australia.  The difference in respect of some other countries is even
higher. We will not get over our current account deficit and we will not be able to
increase our wages in New Zealand and grow our export economy unless we address
these problems.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, it is an
interesting little story that Mr Parker runs. We have actually had in this country an
independent Reserve Bank focu sed on fighting inflation since 1989. It was introduced,
of course, by a Labour Government, and in all other respects they are ashamed of it on
the other side of the House, but nevertheless, the members of the Labour Party seem to
be a little bit happier with this one.
That model is based on transparency and independence, and Labour has now
decided—or, more particularly, Mr Parker has now decided —to pretend you can
simultaneously have low inflation, low interest rates, a low exchange rate, low house
prices, and a current account surplus all because David Parker magically says that is
possible.
The only way you can have a few of those things is if you allow more inflation in
New Zealand. Actually, it is a law of physics that, actually, unless you have an
independent monetary policy, then you will have more inflation. Labour is basically
saying that if it is going to change this thing, then the interest rates would be different,
and if the interest rates are different, then that means more inflation. All inflation does is
destroy the savings of New Zealanders, it makes it more difficult for businesses and
consumers to invest, and it sets off wage and price spirals. And, interestingly, it hits the
people who are struggling the most the hardest.
As one commentator said after Labour had announced its policy: “It’s deeply bizarre
that the Labour Party would actually actively promote policies that would harm the
worst off in society the most.” That is what Labour’s proposed softening of its attitude
to inflation wo uld achieve, which, of course, brings me to the small issue of the
KiwiSaver idea, the interest rate jack -up idea —the “big tool” that Mr Parker likes to
refer to—which I respond to today. But the moment you think about that, it falls apart,
because housing is less than half of New Zealanders’ debt. The rest is companies, credit
cards, farmers, councils, and Government agencies.
Apparently, Labour is going to tell businesses and councils to carry on borrowing
and spending, because wage and salary earners wi ll be forced to have more money
taken out of their take-home pay to do the belt tightening for them. Weirdly, Labour has
still not come up with any sort of indication of how much it would require people to put
into their KiwiSaver accounts to offset a 1 pe rcent increase in interest rates. So here we
are—I think it was the beginning of May that this thing came out —6 weeks down the
line and Labour is still shtoom on any suggestion of what the actual trade -off would be
18538 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
between rising interest rates and forcing  people to put more money in their KiwiSaver
accounts.
Well, over on this side of the House we actually did the exercise. We reckon that to
get 1 percent, Labour would have to increase the KiwiSaver contributions by around 6
percent. Those members are out  there today saying that they are already going to
increase your KiwiSaver—

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Rubbish! Making it up.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: It is true. And if it is not true, then the Opposition should
actually come up with some numbers.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: You’ve made it up.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: They are not made -up numbers. They are actually worked
out, and what we know is that the Opposition has come up with nothing. So here we are
debating the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act and the Reserve Bank, and the Labour
Party is proposing to throw away the independent control of inflation. It is talking about
this “big tool”, this weird big tool, which, apparently, magically can keep interest rates
under c ontrol while boosting people’s KiwiSaver rates, and it has no idea how that
works.
It is actually embarrassing in a debate about Crown entities for that sort of ridiculous
policy-on-the-fly rubbish that the Opposition has come up with. So, fundamentally, the
good thing about the Reserve Bank policy is that it controls inflation. Inflation is very
tough, particularly on those people who are struggling the most in society, and what we
know is that the Labour Party would change that. We know it would relax th e control of
inflation, and we know that its monetary policy approach is to force people to have
more money taken out of their take -home pay, but Labour says: “Don’t worry. You’ll
all get it back when you are 65.”
So while you are sitting there with your families, under Labour Party - type inflation
conditions—which, as we know, is about 8 percent, which is what it was at the last
election, or higher again; those were the high inflationary times —Labour will be saying
to New Zealanders: “Don’t worry. The so lution is to whip some more money out of
your pay. Don’t worry that prices are going up. You will feel it for, oh, I don’t know,
maybe a year, but the good news is that in the long run” —the very long run, when you
are 65—“you will get a little bit of it ba ck.” That is those members’ answer, and what a
load of rubbish.
Report noted.
New Zealand Transport Agency

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: It is great to be here debating the
financial review of the New Zealand Transport Agency, because just yesterday we had
the Minister of Transport, the Hon Gerry Brownlee, give one of his famous Morning
Report interviews. It was a cracker, actually. I am t hinking of putting together, as a
campaign fund-raiser, a collected edition CD of Gerry Brownlee’s transport interviews
on Morning Report, because they are quite remarkable—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: And the EQC ones.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: That is right —and the Earthquake Commission interviews. He
said some amazing things, actually. When asked about the draft Government Policy
Statement on Land Transport 2014/15 - 2024/25, he said: “The focus is not on roads.”
As an example of deny, divert, and  obfuscate, it was one of the classics, Mr Brownlee,
and I want to compliment you on that. The other cracker quotation from Gerry

items.speaker: Brownlee was
items.text: “Until this Government came along, no one was much interested in
walking and cycling.” It is great to see Gerry Brownlee taking responsibility —taking
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18539
personal credit —for the growth in public interest in and support for walking and
cycling.
I mention the Government policy statement because the very interesting thing about
this is that the Government policy statement  sets out the Government’s transport
priorities for the next decade. The reason it is relevant to this debate is that the
Government’s policy statement for the next decade is almost exactly the same as the
Government’s priorities that we have had to put up  with for nearly the last 6 years. It is
all about roads, roads, roads with this Government. What we see in the Government
policy statement is a continuation of its spending more than $1 billion every year on its
new mega -motorway projects. If you look at the funding there, it has allocated $20
billion to State highways and only a fifth of that —or $4 billion —over the same period
to public transport, walking, and cycling. A full 87 percent of the Budget projections in
the Government policy statement has been  allocated to roads—39 percent for new State
highways, which are predominantly the roads of National Party significance —10
percent for public transport, and only 1 percent for walking and cycling. Yet Gerry
Brownlee goes on Morning Report and says that thi s is not all about roads. Well, this
Government is obsessed with building new motorways. It has poured more than a
billion dollars every year into these projects at the expense of the regions, at the expense
of the maintenance of local roads, and at the ex pense of public transport in our large
cities.
Why does this matter? Why does it matter that the Government has this incredibly
unbalanced transport policy? Well, one of the reasons it matters is that it is structuring
into our transport system, into the export supply chain, gross inefficiencies. This
Minister and this Government believe that every freight task can be done —no matter
what it is and no matter where it is going —most efficiently by being hauled on huge
trucks on brand new, gold-plated, and mostly duplicate motorway projects. It refused to
build a truly sustainably and efficient freight supply chain in this country by investing in
and getting the best out of all the different modes of transport and all the different pieces
of the transport syste m. So what it refused to do and what the next Labour -led
Government will do is take an intelligent and clinical look at how the ports, how coastal
shipping, and how rail can work together with the roading system to achieve much
better connectivity and get our products to market in the most efficient and sustainable
way.
But this Government is not interested in that, and what was, I think, particularly
revealing was that the Government policy statement on transport cannot, under its own
terms of reference, talk about coastal shipping, about rail, and about ports. Critical
elements of the transport system are separated out from the Government’s main policy -
making tool and its main statement of priorities, because the transport system basically
exists in these  silos. The Government likes it that way. Gerry Brownlee likes it that
way, because he does not want to have to consider those other important parts of the
transport system. He is not interested in rail, he is not interested in coastal shipping and
ports; it is all about roads. Under the system that we have got, under the transport
system that this Government is perfectly happy with, New Zealand Transport Agency is
the big road builder. It is the deliverer of our transport policy. That will change under
the next Labour Government.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: I would like to just congratulate
the Minister of Transport on the great work that he has done in this area over the la st 3
years. He is an exceptional Minister, and always welcome in the Waikato. He can come
there any time, unlike the Opposition members, who never come to the Waikato, and
when they do come, they do not have anything to say of any consequence.
18540 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: You can’t say we never come and then say what we do when we
do come.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, that member is pretty much a non -event when Labour
members do come, if they do come.
As for Mr Twyford, we hear this speech every year from the Labour Party, saying
how it is going to have a multimodal solution, using all the terminology about “we’re
investing in roads and rail and maritime and all those things, and public transport.”
There is all that talk but no actual, definite de tails about what the Labour Party wants to
do. Why does it not come out and actually say what it wants to do? There is a reason,
New Zealanders, why Labour members do not come out and say what they want to do.
It is because they know that what they want to  do is in direct conflict with the Green
Party, and they cannot afford to have that fight before the election.
Who runs transport policy in the left wing? It is the Green Party. It is Julie Anne
Genter. Julie Anne runs it, not Phil Twyford.

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Order! Members’ full names.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: If you were a betting person, you would put your money on
Julie Anne Genter to have more power over the transport portfolio than Mr Phi l
Twyford—the nice guy that he may be. That is the reality of the Labour Party policy. It
is all hot air and talk and no commitment. Will it commit to the Waikato Expressway?
No, it will not commit to the Waikato Expressway. It will not commit to building that,
because it knows that Julie Anne Genter has gone out and said that she wants to review
that project. Julie Anne Genter, when asked about that project a mere 2 weeks ago, said
that the Green Party would review that project.
What about other roads of national significance around the country? What about the
Pūhoi road, which I am sure Mike Sabin will want to know about? What is the Greens’
policy on that? What is the Greens’ policy on Transmission Gully? The Green members
will tell us the next time. The y will be open and honest and tell you what they think.
They will go out there and say that they are not doing them. The Labour Party, in effect,
will not be doing them either. So New Zealanders need to listen to what the Green Party
is saying, because that is the Labour Party transport policy.
Then we have New Zealand First, the other arm in the Labour - left-wing attempt to
try to get seats in Parliament. It came up with this transport policy that I would love to
see rearticulated in this Chamber. We had  a transport debate last week, and we had the
New Zealand First transport policy that was for passenger rail from every city in New

items.speaker: Zealand
items.text: passenger rail from Wanganui to Wellington, passenger rail from Hamilton to
Auckland, passenger rail from Timaru to  Christchurch—passenger rail everywhere and
anywhere.
Denis O’Rourke: That’s right.

items.speaker: DAVID BENNETT
items.text: Oh, and all these trains would have been built in New Zealand,
of course, under New Zealand First policy. But I want to see New Zealand First come
up here and say what it said at that transport conference. Denis O’Rourke has got his
chance to come out and say it. How is New Zealand going to afford a train from
Wanganui to Wellington? Tell me that. How are we going to afford tha t? That is what
the New Zealand First Policy is. The Green Party policy actually pales in comparison
with New Zealand First’s policy. The Green Party used to be the party of trains, but
now it is New Zealand First that is the party of trains, and the Green  Party now has to
up its game to match that.
On this side of the House, on the Government side, we see a party that has good,
strong leadership, and a Minister who has taken a balanced approach to transport
funding. Not only have we invested heavily in the  infrastructure of our roads, but we
have invested heavily in our rail network
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18541
We have invested in the KiwiRail Turnaround Plan. We have invested in public
transport options in Auckland, and we have a plan for that public transport going
forward. That is a  balanced approach. We have taken action in the maritime and
aviation areas where it has been required as well. That is what transport policy demands,
not the Julie Anne Genter model of transport policy. Thank you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is fantastic to follow in the wake of the
chair of the Transport and Industrial Relations Committee. It is strong chairmanship that
he shows, as one would expect with such a strong and high -performing Minister of
Transport as Gerry Brownlee, of course. What a great team. What a great team the
National Party has put together on this side of the House. I just want to pick up on a
couple of comments that were made by the new comedic home for evening come dy on
the Labour Party, Phil Twyford, who talks about the comment that it is not just about
roads.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Say that again, Mike. I missed it.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: I forget exactly what I said. We will go back to the Hansard.
It is not just about roads; it is actually about transportation on multiple levels. If there
is one thing that we can say about the efforts of this Government in terms of
transportation, what we have actually done is we have unwound decades of under -
investment in some of the key areas of our transport infrastructure. Significant money
has been put into KiwiRail. A Labour Government that sold off —[Interruption] Sorry,
what is the member Tracey Martin saying? I cannot quite hear. [ Interruption] No,
Tracey Martin h as got that wrong, because you will find that Marsden Point is in the
Whangarei electorate. But is that an important piece of infrastructure? Absolutely, and
that is why we are making sure when we have discussions with the councils that are
looking at the Ports of Auckland, Tauranga, and Marsden Point that they understand the
needs of the transportation infrastructure there. If the member wants to come up to
Whangarei and have a wee discussion on it, I am sure the new member in Whangarei
would be happy to allude to that.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Phil Heatley is still there. Don’t be so horrible.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: No, I am talking post-election, of course, Ms Dyson.
We are a forward -looking party, and the reality is that when we look at the
Government policy statement—let us take just one little small snippet of the programme
of work that has been going on here, the Pūhoi to Wellsford road. As David Bennett has
mentioned, the Greens and Labour have both signalled that road will come out. They
say they will get rid of that project. This Government has fast -tracked the consenting
process, alongside Auckland Council, which has also, 16 votes to four, recognised the
importance of that road. It is a trade and economic highway to what is the fastest -
growing economy in the country. The Northland economy is the fastest -growing and
strongest-growing economy in the country. We know that $800 million of primary
industries, particularly, is trundling down that road on an annual basis. That is a
significant co ntribution to this country’s economic fortunes, and this Government is
investing in that. In fact, this Government is ensuring that that programme is given
every opportunity to move forward as quickly as possible.
When that was signalled in Northland, I c an tell members across this House that it
was absolutely strongly heralded as a fantastic initiative because of the importance of
that road. It is not just about the road in itself. It is about the signals it sends about the
economy of Northland and the op portunities that exist for other businesses to be
involved in growing that economy and being a part of that economy. The road will take
some time to build, but already, with the interest in activity, people are looking north
and they are looking north beca use here is a region that is attached to the nation’s
largest economy, in Auckland, and that is a vital link. If we look across the roads of
18542 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
national significance programme, that is exactly what we see. We see the arterial
routes—the routes that are so often used by so much of the economy of this country. We
are ensuring that the under-investment that has occurred for far too long in this nation is
actually being caught up with and we are investing where we are going to free up and
ensure that that transportation of our economy is going to move far more effectively.
We can talk about public transport all we like, but —I do not know; call me old -
fashioned—I think buses tend to use roads as well. I have not seen too many “hover -
buses”. Perhaps the Green Party might want to introduce some of those into the mix —I
am not sure. Whether they are highways, motorways, freeways, or single lane roads,
anything with wheels on it uses them, even cycles, which I know the Green Party, of
course, is very, very interested in.  The point is that what the Government has done is
establish a programme of work across many facets of our transportation networks to
ensure that where the bottlenecks exist, where the challenges in that network exist, we
are absolutely investing in that a nd investing ahead of the curve, which is taking some
investment to catch up on because, as I said, there has been a consistent under -
investment in that. So what we are seeing—

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: This is a financial review of
the activities of the New Zealand Transport Agency over the past year. Naturally, when
considering that, one might look back and one might look forward. I accept that. But I
was particularly distressed today by some of the comments in the speech offered to the
House by the Labour spokesperson on transport. What he seems to have missed is that
this process is guided —that is, the process of the Government policy statement and the
work of the New Zealand Transport Agency —by the Land Transport Management Act
2003. I would suggest that if he is to be an effective spokesperson, he should go and
read that Act so that he does not make some of the extraordinary statements that he
made in the House this afternoon.

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: Overdue for reform.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: What I would like to hear from him at some point is
that if he thinks that Act needs to be reformed, he starts to spell out what it is, because
all I hear from him is about what Labour is not going to do, should the unlikely event of
its receiving the opportunity to sit on the Treasury benches occur. Labour is not going to
continue with the roads of national significance programme. It is not going t o invest in
cycle networks, as we have. It is not going to invest in pedestrian opportunities, as we
have, and it is not going to have an arrangement that allows local communities to
choose where they spend some of the funding that comes from the National Land
Transport Fund on their own projects. Anyone can stand in this House and tell people
what they are not going to do; to talk about what you are doing and what a Government
is doing is a different matter.
We have, over the last short while, since 2012,  spent a staggering $945 million —a
billion dollars, effectively —on public transport. That has been matched by local
authorities, which have contributed another $770 million. So there you see a huge
commitment to public transport for a very small part of th e transport task required in
New Zealand. We have further said that if we can see that the demand for public
transport is on the rise, we will be there to fund it. I want to know whether, in fact, the
Labour Party is proposing that it would do away with th e $800 million package that we
have put together for Auckland to bring forward some of its roading projects. The
answer would be yes, because Labour does not like roads. It somehow thinks that New
Zealand should return to a sort of strange community where we do not make use of
roads.
When it comes to KiwiRail, over a billion dollars so far has been reinvested in that
company, trying to give it the opportunity to contribute more to the freight task
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18543
throughout New Zealand. But the reality is that the rails d o not run into many of the
rural communities in New Zealand where the productivity that comes off our agrarian
economy is carried out. So there has to be an ability to move freight by road. What I
want to do this afternoon is congratulate the management of  KiwiRail on collaborating
with road freight companies throughout the country to get a better synergy between the
opportunity to move goods over long distances on rail with the capacity to take
significant loads by truck to the farm gate and beyond. When Mr Twyford stands up and
says there is no big thinking going on here, I have got to tell him that out in the wide
world people do not necessarily look to the Opposition spokesman’s office to see that
big thinking. Thank God they do not, because there is none.
The reality is that we have a dynamic transport industry in New Zealand and we have
a Government that is making investments in the transport infrastructure to ensure that it
prospers along with the rest of the economy for years to come. It was the Roma ns who
first worked out that if you want to have a dynamic economy, provide roads, and that is
what we are doing.
Report noted.
Earthquake Commission
Hon NICKY WAGNER (Associate Minister for Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery): I am very pleased to speak in this debate on the report on the Earthquake
Commission. I speak in this debate as the member of Parliament for Christchurch
Central. I want to talk a bout the operations of the Earthquake Commission in
Christchurch. Christchurch people love to hate the Earthquake Commission. We love to
hate the Earthquake Commission because in the last 3 years things have been very
tough in Christchurch. Nothing has bee n simple about our earthquakes, and the
Earthquake Commission has had to work under very difficult circumstances.
But we are also very aware that New Zealand is in a unique insurance situation
because of the Earthquake Commission. When you look at other s imilar earthquake -
prone countries, especially those around the Pacific Rim —the US and Japan —only
about 15 to 20 percent of ordinary citizens have their homes insured, simply because of
the cost, and no one’s land is insured at all. I visited San Francisco in 2012 and I was
horrified to see properties, homes, that had been rebuilt on the area of the land that had
been very hard hit during the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. These homes were mostly
uninsured, and, certainly, nobody had land insurance. They were uninsured because of
the cost of insurance. If you live in an earthquake -prone country, unless it happens to be
New Zealand, it is prohibitive to pay for insurance for normal families. That situation
would be the same here, except that the Earthquake Commi ssion takes the very high -
risk first $100,000 of risk, so that supplementary insurance is affordable. So, although
we love to hate the Earthquake Commission in Christchurch, I cannot imagine what it
would be like in Christchurch if 80 to 85 percent of ou r homes were uninsured and our
land was also unprotected.
I acknowledge that there have been issues with Earthquake Commission claims. The
size of the event, the number of earthquakes, the fact that most people have multiple
claims, the management structu re of multi -unit properties, and the tough environment
for everyone who works in our communities have made it particularly hard. The
Earthquake Commission has had to scale up very fast. But I sincerely believe that
everyone in the Earthquake Commission is working hard to settle claims and we are
now seeing real progress. Ultimately, we have to remember that every last claim will be
paid out and that the Earthquake Commission will continue to provide New Zealanders
with insurance long after Christchurch homes are restored and our city is rebuilt.
18544 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
Let us now have a look at the Earthquake Commission’s statistics. We can get a good
idea of the size of the task in hand and of the progress that has been made. Since
February 2011 the Earthquake Commission has had 1.64 million interactions with
homeowners. That is equivalent to dealing with every single person who lives in
Auckland and in Northland. The assessors have done 750,000 assessments or
reassessments after multiple earthquakes, which is equivalent to two as sessments for
every single person who lives in Christchurch. The Earthquake Commission has paid
out $7.4 billion including GST.
Let us have a look at how those claims pan out. Eighty -three percent of cash
settlement claims have been completed. Ninety -one percent of all claims under $15,000
have been resolved. Seventy -five percent of claims between $15,000 and $100,000 are
settled. And 90 percent of overlapped claims are settled. That means that 90 percent of
those claims have moved on to the insurance companies for a rebuild or a repair. On top
of that, 78 percent of properties in the Canterbury Home Repair Programme are
complete.
I really do want to focus on vulnerable customers, because this is a priority area of
the Earthquake Commission and it is an area that concerns us all. Eighty -six percent of
the claims of vulnerable customers are complete, and the Earthquake Commission is
absolutely committed to fixing the homes of the rest of these people. One of the issues
that we have had in Christchurch is that it has been very difficult to get to the people
who most need our help. If you compare an earthquake like the Christchurch—

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: One of the few things that I would agree with Nicky
Wagner on is that things have been tough in Christchurch. Research out today from
Healthy Christchurch shows that 65 percent of Chri stchurch residents reported feeling
tired in 2014, and that is a 10 percent increase on 2012. Certainly, dealing with the
Earthquake Commission and with insurance claims has contributed to that feeling of
tiredness, particularly when often you have got ver y poor communication by the
Earthquake Commission, so that at least 5 percent of Christchurch households have had
to resort to the Official Information Act to try to get some basic information out of the
commission. The commission has got a very ambitious target of completing all repairs
on earthquake-damaged homes by the end of this year. That is another more than 25,000
full repairs that it is yet to do. The claim that that will be done by the end of this year
makes many Christchurch residents laugh out l oud, when they are still dealing with that
dance and interaction with the Earthquake Commission.
If we had a Green Party in Government, we would have had the Earthquake
Commission and Housing New Zealand working alongside each other to tackle the
housing crisis. We know that the Minister has denied that there is a housing crisis in
Christchurch, despite the fact that there are regular reports in the press of people surfing
on friends’ couches, sleeping in garages, and sleeping in cars. We do have a housing
crisis because so many people have had to move out of their homes in the red zone or
because their homes are uninhabitable because of earthquake damage or flooding
vulnerability. If we had more joined -up thinking, we would have had Housing New
Zealand building more State houses. We would have had a progressive homeownership
scheme where people in those homes could progressively buy them from the State
during their time in the house, without getting a big mortgage and without heavy debt,
just as many of our  parents did using the former family benefits. If we had joined -up
thinking, we would have had the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme going
at full strength, not being savagely cut, as National has done.
The Earthquake Commission has a winter welln ess programme, and that is a
response to the fact that many homes in Christchurch have lost their primary heating
source through damage to chimneys, fireplaces, and woodburners. Certainly, the
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18545
Earthquake Commission programme has meant that several thousand  homes across
Christchurch have had new heat pumps installed.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: All right, 20,000, Minister —thank you. But the Earthquake
Commission and the Government have missed the opportunity t o substantially improve
the housing stock in Christchurch through a full Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart
programme. It has missed the opportunity to substantially reduce the 600,000 homes
across New Zealand that are cold, that are draughty, that contribute  to health issues for
children, and that see kids being sick and off school and their parents taking time off
work. We want to ensure that all our homes are warm, dry, secure, and healthy. The
Government gave the cold shoulder to Christchurch by making a m ajor cut in the Warm

items.speaker: Up New Zealand
items.text: Heat Smart programme, so it was not working alongside the
Earthquake Commission to make the most of the crisis in Christchurch. It could have
ensured that there was more subsidy assistance available so that people could  insulate
their homes at the same time as they were undertaking major earthquake repairs. The
Green Party’s Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart programme would do that by
providing subsidies for wall insulation.
Instead, what did the Earthquake Commission do? Initially, it opposed the betterment
of homes and then it allowed it, but homeowners have to cover the cost of putting in
wall insulation while full repairs are under way. The Green Party would provide
assistance to enable that to be more affordable. That  whole scheme would cost about
$35 million in Christchurch for making sure that we improve our housing stock, we
build it back better post -earthquake, and we do not simply replace like with like and
miss the opportunity that we have to create much warmer, drier, and more healthy
homes. The Earthquake Commission has done a bit with the heat pumps but it has not
used the opportunity that the earthquakes have provided to provide more insulated
homes so that everyone has a warm, dry, and healthy home.
National has significantly reduced the Warm Up New Zealand: Heat Smart scheme.
Initially, in the first 3 years there were over 200,000 houses insulated; now its target is
only 46,000 homes.

items.speaker: Hon RU TH DYSON
items.text: Can I first of all say that it is
blindingly obvious to anyone that the Earthquake Commission has faced a big job and it
is in no one’s interest to do as the current member for Christchurch Central did and
assume that challenges to the current system are a proposal to get rid of the Earthquake
Commission. That is a nonsense conclusion that Nicky Wagner reached and I know that
nobody is proposing that. But we cannot deny the fact that the level of arrogance,
bullying, and incomp etence displayed by the Earthquake Commission is having
anything other than a negative impact on residents in Canterbury. I think the same goes
for the Minister responsible for the Earthquake Commission, actually. Nobody has
denied that the Minister, who h as got several portfolios —perhaps two too many —has
got a big job in front of him. Nobody is arguing about that. But it does not mean that
when somebody challenges it, questions it, or says that this is clearly not going right, we
should be subject to bully ing or abuse. That shows a level of being out of touch with
what people in Canterbury are going through.
I want to touch on just three points briefly. The first is the self -imposed time frame
that the Earthquake Commission has set for settling claims. The  second is its method of
cash settlements, and the concerns I have about that. The third is in relation to multi-unit
dwellings. I think that people in Canterbury deserve certainty, they deserve support, and
they need to know that the Government and Govern ment departments and agencies of
Government are on their side and working for a positive resolution of the huge tragedy
that everyone has felt in one way or another. It has affected different people in different
18546 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
ways; everyone in Canterbury has been affect ed by the earthquakes. What they need
now is a Government that is clearly on their side and that can help them move to a
positive solution and outcome.
Let me go back to the first of the three points —the self -imposed time frame. Ian
Simpson has written to us all again. He is the chief executive of the Earthquake
Commission. He has just written to us and said: “I’ve made a commitment to you to fix
your home or settle your claim by December of this year.” Then he says: “While I’m
confident of our 2014 target,  if we have to run into 2015, we’ll do so.” Well, that is
hugely reassuring. We are committed to fixing everything by the end of 2014, but if we
do not make it, we go into next year. Well, what a reassurance that is! This is in writing
from the chief executive. That gives us no reassurance, Minister, and I think you should
be on his case and on the case of the chair of the Earthquake Commission to give us
correspondence and give us time frames that mean something or stop wasting the
stamps. This sort of dribble does not help anyone.
The second thing I want to talk about is cash settlements. In this same letter, Ian

items.speaker: Simpson says
items.text: “We will not be using large -scale cash settlement to meet our December
target. We will continue fixing homes until the job’s done. ” That is just untrue. The
Earthquake Commission is bullying people, including the most vulnerable people, into
taking cash settlements, and I think it is an outrage and it is about time that Minister
Gerry Brownlee stood up to its bullying tactics and sai d that cash settlements should be
an offer, not a compulsion, and people who do not want to opt out should not be bullied
into doing it. I have got two examples. One is a 95 -year-old constituent of mine who
still has plywood cladding on the outside of her home—a well -under-cap, multi -unit
dwelling—and the house next door is going to be demolished. She has been told in
writing that the Earthquake Commission has yet to develop its policy on multi -unit
dwelling, so she is going into her fourth winter in an unc lad home and it is cold, Mr
Brownlee. It is just cold. She is not blaming you. She is pretty generous, but I think that
the buck stops with the Minister and she should not have to do that. She has been told
she can cash settle or join a very long queue. Sh e is 95 years of age. She is competent.
She is able. But it is the Earthquake Commission’s job to fix her house, not hers.
I have got another example that I will just briefly read out to the Committee. This is
from a senior claims manager at the Earthquake Commission, who says to a person who
does not want to cash settle: “I will again insert our rights to cash settle” and quoting
section 29 of the Act. A bullying threat to cash settle, not an offer, is not good enough,
Mr Brownlee. The Minister needs to take responsibility for stopping that practice.
Hon GERRY BROWNLEE (Minister responsible for the Earthquake
Commission): I should respond to some of  those comments offered by the Hon Ruth
Dyson. The first point I would like to make, though, is that the Earthquake Commission
has to date settled 141,000 claims and that is an 83 percent settlement rate. Yes, Ruth
Dyson is right to say that multi -units pr esent a problem. Part of the problem is that
where you have multiple buildings —these are blocks of flats, apartment buildings, or
anything else—then there can be multiple insurers over them. There is also the problem,
which Ruth Dyson illustrated very well  by talking about her constituent, whom I would
like to know a little bit more about, I must say, because that does cause me some
concern—

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: What, so you can abuse me again? No way, José.

items.speaker: Hon GERRY BROWNLEE
items.text: Well, you see, there is the problem. I genuinely stand
in the Committee and say that if you have got that person and they need help, I would
like to be there to help them, and I am told that all that is going to happen is that the
member will get abusive . This is ridiculous. Here we are. Here is the deal. That lady
clearly has got a problem with her house, no doubt about that. But what Ruth Dyson
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18547
said is that the property next door is going to be demolished, so that means that the
adjoining house—if we look at this box here with all those boxes, that is a multi -unit. I
do not know where in the units her house is, but if one has to be demolished next to it, it
is going to cause damage to her house. There is no question about that. So the question
has to be who pays, where, and what insurance gets triggered.
The worst we have got is a block of 43 flats or apartments all together where there
are 16 insurers. The insurers are all saying: “Well, hang on a minute. My responsibility
is for this bit over here. If you fix your bit, you’re going to cause me more expense.” So
behind the scenes there has been a huge effort to get insurers to try to sort this out. In
the end, guess who is truly responsible for this appalling problem? It is the legal
fraternity of Canterbury, frankly, because there have been body corporate laws in place
and, repeatedly, lawyers have conveyed properties ignoring the body corporate laws —
willy nilly ignoring the body corporate laws. So when I see some of these flash lawyers
around town start pontificating on what the Earthquake Commission should be doing or
what private insurers should be doing, I just put it back on them and ask about how
many multi-units that particular lawyer has conveyed in their time, ignoring those body
corporate rules.
All I am saying here is that this is a very real problem. It is not something that you
can fix by standing up and screaming and yelling at people; it takes a lot of work to get
through it. We are making those commitments and we are settling those particu lar
issues bit by bit. I have got to say that coming into the House or going on the TV or
getting in the newspaper and having a flick at some of the Earthquake Commission
people is far too easy. They are Canterbury residents themselves. Many of them have
got damaged houses themselves. They know what the reality of living in the city is, and
they come to work every day and deal with people’s problems. I admire them for doing
that, and, frankly, the statistics show that they are doing a very good job.
I want to briefly finish on the comment from Eugenie Sage, when she talked about
the latest wellness index from Canterbury. Firstly, the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery
Authority contributed to that cost, as did private insurers, and I understand that the
Earthquake Commission did, as well. So we want to know what the situation is. The
international literature tells us that the third year after an event is always the hardest. We
need to know the extent of that problem, and we are not walking away from it. There
are services available for people who are suffering those stresses in their lives. We
know that getting people through this is going to be settling all of the Earthquake
Commission issues and getting people back into as much as possible of the groove that
their life used to be. That is the commitment the Government has made through the
Earthquake Commission, and we have not walked away from any responsibility we
have in Canterbury one little bit. It is disappointing that people find a need to
misrepresent situations to try to paint the worst picture of them.
I say again to Ruth Dyson to tell me what that poor woman’s situation is. I would
like to look at it because I think something more should be done for her. To suggest that
the member has let her sit for 3 years in a cold house and has not told someone who can
do something about it is equally disgraceful.
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : The Government’s handling of the whole
earthquake recovery in Canterbury has been a test for both the Earthquake Commission
and the Government. After more than 3 years, the conclusion has to be that although
some good things have been done, there is still far too much that has not been done and
still far too many issues t hat are unresolved. Neither the commission nor the
Government has scored a pass mark, and their report cards should read “must do better”.
The Budget forecast a surplus of close to half a billion dollars, but at the same time the
budget for Canterbury eart hquake matters was reduced by about half a billion dollars.
18548 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
That indicates that the budget for Canterbury earthquakes was reduced not because that
was possible given the progress of recovery projects —or, more accurately, the lack of
progress—but because th is part of the Government’s Budget was an easy manipulation
to create an artificial surplus for election-year purposes.
That has been confirmed within the last few days, when the Prime Minister indicated
that far from it being possible to spend less, the Government will most likely have to
face an additional $5 billion or more for the rebuild over coming years, as the overall
cost has escalated. The Government is simply not being transparent about the real size
of the contribution it will need to make. Thi s issue alone makes its claimed Budget
projections and the forecast surplus an absolute farce.
Most people in Canterbury are concerned about the slowness of so many aspects of
the rebuild and the dilatory way the Government and its agencies have handled t he
needs of the city. Infrastructure repairs are taking far too long. Demolitions are still not
done after 3 years or more. Rebuilds are only just getting started. Planning gives little
cause for confidence to people who need to make decisions about their investments.
Insurers are getting away with blue murder. Decisions on Port Hills properties are still
not made, and the list goes on.
But one of the worst performances by all agencies has been the failure to deal with
flooding in one part of Christchurch in particular. This was a problem well known soon
after the earthquakes, but 3 years later and several floods later, there has still been no
action on the ground. That is not good enough from the Government, and it is not good
enough for the Government to blame the city council either. Flooding is clearly an
earthquake effect and it is a Government responsibility. The planning should have been
completed and the work started by now to relieve those flooding problems. Purchase
offers without red zoning for th ose to whom the work would not be effective or would
be too slow should have been made by now. This is a disgraceful absence of action by
Government agencies, and there will likely be more flooding of homes still to come this
winter.
Another disgraceful p erformance has been over compensation for red -zoned,
uninsured, or bare land. The offer of 50 percent of 2007 valuations was never justified
or justifiable. The courts have now said so, and now the red zone quake outcasts have
been given leave to apply to the Supreme Court to have the whole red -zoning process
for all of Christchurch deemed illegal. That would be catastrophic as a result for the
Government and for New Zealand as a whole. The hearing is in July. The Supreme
Court bench will not be easily infl uenced by political considerations. So, not only is the
50 percent offer clearly illegal but we face the prospect that the whole red -zoning
concept may be illegal, too, with all the ramifications that that will have.
If that is not bad enough, the Port Hi lls people still waiting for a decision have been
told that they will have to wait even longer until the court has made a decision on red
zoning. These people are still suffering. They have been suffering for 3 years or more.
They are paying mortgages, a p roportion of rates, and rents all at the same time. How
would you, Mr Chairman, like to be in that position? The Government and its agencies
should have made better decisions in the first place.
Report noted.
AgResearch

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: AgResearch is mismanaging
public funds, and at the same time it is losing some of our top scientific talent. It is
proceeding with a $100 million restructure despite evidence that s hows that it is a waste
of taxpayer funds. The sheepmeat industry has fallen victim to an ideologically driven
board, a plan that is off the rails, and a lame duck Minister of Science and Innovation,
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18549
who has seen the evidence but proven completely unable o r unwilling to hold the board
to account.
Let us have a look at the history. In October 2012 Mr Joyce received the AgResearch
business case. It sat on his desk for 5 months —for 5 months it sat on Mr Joyce’s desk
while he considered whether or not this doc ument was worthy for him to sign off. We
know he then signed it off, and subsequently out came the statement of corporate intent,
which Mr English also signed off. On 30 July 2013 the proposal was put to staff.
Submissions closed in August, and subsequentl y an internal report reviewed the
restructure plan and advised on the way forward. That restructure plan said that many of
AgResearch’s changes were indeed good ideas but that one part made no sense. That
was the part that was about disbanding the Invermay  Agricultural Centre, about pulling
apart a successful hub, a successful commercial model that has generated productivity
gains that amount to pretty much the doubling of sheepmeat productivity in the last 30
years, in order to start from scratch —ditching all the commercial partners, shifting
cities, losing all the scientists, and starting from scratch. That is the case. The internal
review, which received no less than 245 submissions, found that the case for shifting
Invermay did not stack up if AgResearch  wished to achieve its goals of improving
science, improving productivity, and improving on-farm returns.
Then we have a number of intervention points that have arisen since then. The
Minister, Steven Joyce, has been aware of all of these. There was a Pub lic Service
Association (PSA) survey that found that most members would not shift; that top talent
would leave the organisation and would return overseas from whence they came or
would go to other institutions in New Zealand. There was a financial review t hat was
held where the senior management was unable to answer questions and was deceitful in
its responses about the business case. Subsequently, a full business case was released,
but that was not the impression given early on in the process. There has al so been a vote
of no confidence from one of the most significant breeding bodies in the industry, the
Texel breeders of New Zealand. PSA staff at Invermay have unanimously passed a vote
of no confidence in the board and senior management. And then we have the industry—
92 percent of the top ram breeders in New Zealand have opposed this shift and have
said that this makes absolutely no sense at all, and 6 percent abstained. The industry
knows that this is not good for productivity in New Zealand.
But Mr Joyc e, in all of that time, has failed. He has failed to intervene on behalf of
farmers, he has failed to intervene on behalf of science in New Zealand, and he has
failed in his duty to the taxpayer as he sees hundreds of millions of dollars thrown up in
the air for a case that promised only marginal returns. It promised only marginal returns
on its original optimistic assumptions, but those assumptions, as we know, have gone by
the by. We know that the assumptions were that staff would shift in greater numbers
than is currently likely. We know the assumptions were that farms would be sold off;
now the timetable has been pushed back by a year. This is a no -hope case, and the
Minister has failed to intervene on a board that has failed to manage the key risk
identified in its own business case, which is managing the risk of staff loss of those key
scientific staff who are important for productivity improvements of 1 percent per year
ongoing into the future.
Labour has said that we will save Invermay. It is an easy  decision to make. It costs
nothing, and it improves New Zealand’s on -farm productivity. It improves exports for
New Zealand.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: I didn’t hear Iain Lees -Galloway say that. You go to
Palmerston North and say that.

items.speaker: Dr DAVID CLARK
items.text: Mr Woodhouse opposite is, of course, interjecting. He has
toed the party line. He has abandoned the case. He has abandoned logic. He has let the
economic pace—

items.text: I think the member
opposite, David Clark, first raised the issue of lame ducks, and on that note I would first
like to say happy birthday to Trevor Mallard. I understa nd it is a big birthday today.
Secondly, speaking of lame ducks, I see his leader is certainly struggling along in a way

egging the story and, unfortunately, he therefore end s up pretending a case that is not

was all some sort of ideological conspiracy, which, of course, it is not. Fundamentally—

items.text: What about staff retention, Minister?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Oh, be quiet, parrot. Fundamentally —[Interruption] Well,
Mr Chair, I cannot—[Interruption]

items.text: Order! It is sort of an equal-handed kind of set of
events here. The member was perhaps interjecting rather too much, and the Minister on
