items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I apologise for the avian references, Mr Chair. The
situation is simply this: as with many of our Crown research institutes, we have
organisations that have historically had large numbers of assets, many of which are old,
many of which were built around the 1940s or 1950s or inherited from other purposes—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: Invermay are the newest ones; the Minister knows it.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Shh! You will learn something. Many of them have large
amounts of land, but they also need to modernise their facilities to attract new staff, and
that is true of AgResearch, it is true of Plant and Food Research, it is true of Landcare
Research, and so on. And so they are all dealing with the challenge of modernising their
assets to attract not just the existing generation of scientists but the new generation of
scientists that they need to bring into those organisations.
So AgResearch has embarked on this process, and has proposed $100 million worth
of investment in its or ganisation to bring its facilities up to speed and to be modern
facilities. As part of that, it has proposed some changes in the configuration of their
institutes. It never proposed to close Invermay; it has proposed to move some staff
groups. It has been through a long and rigorous process in terms of how it would
finalise those particular proposals. It has landed in a space that I think many critics have
found to be a significant improvement in terms of what it originally proposed, and that
is an importan t part of the process —that you consider and you put forward proposals
and you then respond to the feedback on those.
AgResearch has proposed at this time to retain the Invermay farms and the Ballantrae
Hill Country Research farms. It is going to retain th e existing farm systems deer
researchers at Invermay, which I think makes a lot of sense. It is strengthening the deer
team at Invermay. It is retaining the herd, obviously, at Invermay. It is transferring the
sheep flock from Woodlands to Invermay. It is also combining more with Otago
University staff, which, of course, was the original promise of the Christie Building —
that there would be some Otago University staff located in Invermay. That is now going
to happen. AgResearch has invited some of the region al players that have significant
science teams of their own in the area of environmental science to co-locate at Invermay
as well to build up that. I am hoping that the Southland Regional Council and the Otago
Regional Council take AgResearch up on that op portunity, because I actually think that
would save money for the ratepayers of both regions, as well as building a real centre of
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18551
excellence in this environmental science area. So I think AgResearch has landed
positively.
I appreciate that Mr Clark will never be happy. Interestingly, though, we have not
had a call from Mr Lees -Galloway, who is more than happy about the shifts that
advantage the Palmerston North area. That is one of those things where one end of the
Labour Party speaks out of one side of i ts mouth and the other end speaks out of the
other side. In fact, I think the leader of the Labour Party was in Palmerston North,
committing to the investment in the Palmerston North campus at the same time as his
little friend Mr Clark was down in Dunedin  condemning the change. So I think the
challenge of all of that is that the Labour Party members are basically saying, depending
on which part of the country they are in, that there will either be no change or lots of
change, but they do not need any more money. I think that is another circle they are
going to struggle to square.
The other thing I just note in passing is that this Government is making very big
investments in the science sector in Dunedin. There have been two very positive front -
page articles in the Otago Daily Times in the last couple of weeks. Two new centres of
research excellence are being picked up at Otago University and there is also the
doubling—the doubling —of health research that the university has picked up in the
current year. These are things that, interestingly, have not been greeted with great public
relations—
Report noted.
Callaghan Innovation

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: Last week, when we had the pleasure
of having the Minister of Science and Innovation at the Education and Science
Committee for the estimates hearing, the Minister told us that he did not see the
Government’s investment in Callaghan Innovation as being about creating jobs in the
high-value manufacturing sector. He said that he saw this as being about creating jobs in
the research sector. Well, therein lies the difference between Labour and National and
what we see as the purpose of our investment and putting money into science and
innovation. This is a Minister of Science and Innovation who, I would note, in an earlier
contribution this afternoon called interest rates one of the laws of physics. But I did
think he at least understood innovation and what it takes to translate good ideas and
smart thinking into viable products and companies. But when you are divorcing the
investment that we make as a country and the commitment of taxpayer money into
science and innovation from the creation of high -value jobs in the high -value
manufacturing sector, we have a problem.
National thinks that achieving the Budget surplus is all it is about. But in Labour we
have a grander vision of this. We want to make investments that will lead to New
Zealanders having higher -paying jobs in the future. That is the rea son we invest. If we
stop and pause to consider the name of this very new Crown entity, Callaghan
Innovation, we see that it was the vision of Sir Paul Callaghan that the reason we invest
was to transform our economy for the good of people —not for the good  of companies’
balance sheets but for the good of people and the country as a whole, with the purpose
being to put more money into people’s pockets. This is not a vision that the Minister
shares, clearly.
But what we do have in Callaghan Innovation is a f ledgling Crown entity where,
really, very few people are still sure of exactly what it is, what its mandate is, or what it
is trying to achieve. This is from some of the people who work in the organisation. If we
have a look at what could have been, if we have a look at the Taiwanese model, if we
have a look at the Danish model, we see two very good organisations that had a clear
18552 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
mandate from their Government and a very well -defined mandate of what it was and
what their role was to do. That was the creation  of high-value manufacturing to really
kickstart advanced technology in those countries.
But if we have a look at how we have started out with Callaghan Innovation, we see
that we have Callaghan Innovation trying to sell important intellectual property in  terms
of high -value manufacturing through KiwiStar Optics. We saw that last year. This is
still something that is bubbling along without resolution. But one of the very fearful
things that we have is that this is a Government and a Minister that was willi ng to sell
some of our good ideas offshore and for New Zealand to not realise the benefit of that.
But then we have a look at what is happening to many of the companies that are
receiving grants from within Callaghan Innovation, and actually some of the p recursor
organisations as well. We ask whether what we have put in place has done anything to
turn round the fact that too many of our good ideas get sold and disappear offshore. If
we have a look at the figures released in 2012 by Technology Investment Ne twork, we
see that 32 of our biggest and best high -tech businesses that were created in the last
decade have disappeared overseas, and Callaghan Innovation is not doing anything to
turn that round. We have seen BioDiscovery not being able to receive its fu ll grant,
because, although it would have been awarded it only late last year, it has already made
a decision to take it offshore. We have had LanzaTech make the decision to go offshore.
We have had GreenButton make the decision to go offshore.
So what is it that could have averted that, and is Callaghan Innovation doing it? And
is the Minister pushing along the reason to do it? Well, many of these companies have
pointed to the fact that the places that they are moving to have research and
development tax c redits. If we have a look at LanzaTech, it pointed specifically to the
more positive research environment that it was moving to that would allow its business
to flourish. Instead, what we have is Callaghan Innovation in its fledgling state, and
Labour really hopes that Callaghan Innovation succeeds. When we are in Government,
we will actually put the levers in place to ensure that it can, but now we have many in
the sector, both the science sector and the business sector—

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora. Ngā mihi nui ki a koutou. Kia ora. I rise to
take a call in the Crown entities debate to talk about Callaghan Innovation. How we
build a smart, innovative economy should be one of the key issues we are al l talking
about in the coming months. At the moment, there are some great pockets of excellence
happening across Aotearoa. There is some amazing stuff happening by Kiwi firms, and
I will take my hat off to the Government because there are a few projects th at are
deserving of public support. But what we see is that despite the pockets of excellence,
and despite the amazing, smart, green, innovative thinking that is occurring, it is
happening in a vacuum of Government leadership.
We see a Government that is focused on raw logs, more oil and fracking, and more
milk powder exports overseas. We are on a hiding to nothing as a nation economically
if we continue to simplify our economy and become more dependent on commodity
markets, where the buyers are setting th e price, not us in New Zealand. We risk being
stuck at the bottom of the OECD rankings, where we have declined year after year over
the last three decades, if we stay just on raw logs, milk powder, and oil, and this is
where the Government is literally thr owing tens of millions of dollars of taxpayer
subsidies. So although I celebrate and take my hat off to the pockets of excellence and
the Government support that is occurring, it is tiny compared with the subsidies we see
to the fossil fuel industry and to  the agricultural sector, which is just intensification and
raw commodities.
If we want to build a richer New Zealand with more Kiwis in employment and more
profits staying in New Zealand, we need to keep up the focus on a smart, green,
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18553
innovative economy. This is where the future is. This is where we can build a richer
New Zealand. So although we did not support the initial legislation establishing
Callaghan Innovation, some of the research has been widely supported. Obviously we
did not support it because of the direct ministerial oversight of the Minister sitting in the
chair, the Minister of Science and Innovation, because there is too much control for one
person picking winners. What we want to see is a true competitive process where good
ideas can flow through, not just on the whims of the Minister.
We know we have a national problem when it comes to research and development.
We spend less than half of the OECD average both at the national and commercial
levels. We need to do more. If we look at other  nations like Israel and the amount it is
investing in research and development, we see what we should be striving for that,
because we can build more jobs—more well-paid jobs—when we focus on innovation.
One little policy area in this smart green innovat ion space that the Green Party will
be championing this election is around digital manufacturing, additive manufacturing,
and 3 -D printing. This is something that is, when you hear from the Government
benches, more of a border security threat, because that  is where the officials’ primary
focus is going through the Customs Service. What we want to see is a focus on the
economic potential. I welcome that Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
has finally supported groups like the Titanium Industry De velopment Association with
some assistance to get a 3 -D printer. There is a lot more we can do with the advanced
digital manufacturing sector to grow jobs. It is 16 percent of global GDP —an $11
trillion sector —and it will be taking a bigger slice. With oth er Governments offering
substantial support and substantial leadership, we cannot miss out. We need more
leadership here. We need to set those research and development investment targets
much, much higher.
We need to support those successful Kiwi companie s, particularly in the green
energy space, which the Pure Advantage group of successful Kiwi businesspeople says
is a $6 trillion opportunity for New Zealand to get a slice of. It is a $6 trillion global
market. So a green investment bank would be a great solution in the next term of
Government, and a good green Government will focus on smart green innovation. We
need to not just keep Callaghan Innovation but see a green investment bank established.
We need to support our capital markets with things like a capital gains tax, because it
will focus investment away from the housing speculation market towards the productive
economy. What I want to see is Kiwi families and Kiwi investors investing in Kiwi
businesses. At the moment under the market we are seeing a signal flowing through to
focus on speculation. [ Interruption] I am sure that Jami -Lee Ross does not want to see
more speculation in the Auckland housing market, which is going up and up and up,
driving the interest rate rises that we see under the Key G overnment. There are more
interest rate rises under the Key Government.
What we need to do is see those proper economic signals to invest in productive
businesses, invest in employing Kiwis, and invest in innovation. Ultimately, this is
where Callaghan In novation is doing some good things. Where is it failing? It is the
Minister in the chair. It is the lack of leadership and the lack of focus on a smart green
economy. So this election will be a good opportunity for Kiwis to debate the issues —
smart green innovation or more logs and oil.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: May I say that I do
not think that the last two speakers get out that much. They really do need to get out
some more. I had to laugh at young Gareth Hughes, because he literally said that we
have to encourage the capital markets and we need a capital gain s tax. That is exactly
what he said. The answer to encouraging the capital markets is to tax them more! That
is obviously the answer; how silly of me! He also suggested that the idea of taxing
18554 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
about a quarter of houses would reduce the investment in housin g, whereas at the same
time taxing 100 percent of businesses with a capital gains tax would increase the
investment in businesses. I do not know how that is supposed to work.
He also should have gone to Fieldays last week, because he acted as if the primar y
sector does not innovate. He said that the primary sector needs to innovate more, and
not just sell raw stuff overseas. Well, hello! The news is that actually that is what is
happening. For those of us who did go to Fieldays, I myself was incredibly enco uraged
by the amount of investment in technology and innovation that is going on there, with
the assistance of organisations such as Callaghan Innovation. The farming industry is
now very much a data -driven industry, and the members opposite should get out  more
and actually learn what is going on out there in the actual market place. But the other
thing I would note—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Ask them about a research and development tax credits in the
market place while you are out there.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Oh, by the way, in terms of the whole LanzaTech rubbish,
with the greatest respect, the research and development grants that it was entitled to in
this country were more generous than the ones in the US. The reason it has gone to  the
US is actually what happened under Labour’s watch, when the company was largely
sold offshore while Labour was still around. It hired a chief executive based in the
Midwest of the US and now she wants to put the company there. That is the extent of it .
So, actually, a little bit of work, Megan, would be good in terms of before you pick your
examples as to why things should happen.
What is actually happening is a big increase in private sector research and
development, supported by Callaghan Innovation . We now have $142 million a year
being co -invested alongside private sector companies in research and development
growth grants, and the Opposition still has not woken up to that because it is still
harping on about the policy I think it has announced sev en times now and implemented
once, which is the research and development tax credits. It has got nothing more to say
on innovation at all. That is the entire story in innovation since about 2007. Well,
news—we are in 2014. Something else a little fresh would be helpful.
But the other thing I have got to take up with the member opposite, Megan Woods, is
the issue of this whole thing that companies having international investment is
somehow bad for them. I can tell her that actually a normal part of the innovation
process is that some of the companies are eventually bringing in international investors.
The good news about that, which Ms Woods has overlooked, is that it frees up capital to
invest in more companies, so people like Sam Morgan and so on, who sold their
TradeMe shares, have now invested in a whole range of other companies, and that is
part of what encourages the ecosystem in New Zealand.
My definition of success in innovation is the increase of innovation that occurs in
New Zealand, and that i s what is happening right now in this country. We have had a
big increase in research and development by businesses, and it is continuing to grow.
We have had a big increase in exports by what is known as the high -tech sector, which
is the information and communications technology sector, high-tech manufacturing, and
medium high tech manufacturing. That is increasing. That is a factual reality.

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: How close to the OECD average?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Speaking of the OECD, Mr Hughes was saying that we are
continuing to go down the OECD ladder. Well, I have some news for him, actually. We
stopped going down the OECD ladder as soon as the Labour -Greens crowd went out of
office. We stopped. And, actually, we are now go ing up. The former Prime Minister
Helen Clark talked about being No. 22 in the OECD for years and nothing happened.
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18555
Now, suddenly, we are at 20 and going to 19 because of the work done by this
Government relative to other countries in the OECD.
Here we have a growing high-tech sector that is in really good shape, with more and
more companies listing publicly and more companies being seeded and growing. We
have big support of that from this new entity, Callaghan Innovation. If the member Ms
Woods is unsure of what it is for, I recommend this quite simple page with five bullet
points on it. That would be a good summary for her to start with. We are lifting the
investment in New Zealand’s technology companies and the Opposition needs to bring
itself up to date.
Report noted.
Tertiary Education Commission

items.speaker: COLIN KING
items.text: It is a pleasure to talk about the
achievements of the Government and the Tertiary Education Commission at this
particular time. Just for those who are listening, we are talking about the Tertiary
Education Commission, which fundamentally provides the stakeholder funds to the
universities, the wānangas, the private training establishments, the industry training
organisations, and the polytechs. It has been very important to appreciate that on
coming into Government, National recognised that that area was grossly over -supported
but without the products and results coming out. So the Government is to be
commended for the wo nderful job that it has done in focusing especially the training
providers into being accountable to the taxpayer for the dollars that are invested in
there—the better part of $2 billion. That has been the work of the Government and the
Minister for Tertia ry Education, Skills and Employment in focusing those particular
providers on the job at hand.
It is very important that the taxpayer dollars are spent wisely and that the intention of
the tertiary education strategy is implemented, and we certainly see t hat over the last
two Budgets that has certainly been the case: further improvement. I cast my mind back
to when I heard a comment in one of the interviews that we had with the Minister with
regard to how much more blood you can screw out of a stone. I tho ught to myself:
“What a wonderful analogy.” That is the difference between the Opposition and the
Government. The Government, on this side of the Chamber, has extracted better value
for the taxpayer dollar out of the tertiary education sector —not only in o ne area but
across the whole gambit within the Tertiary Education Commission. It is also focused
very much on what the Government can do to pull levers to stimulate and attract people
into those areas that are very important for the continual growth in sci ence and
innovation of our economy. That is what it has been doing.
There has been further investment in those “STEM” subjects —the scienc es, the
technologies, the engineering, and the mathematics. All those things are certainly
opportunities that should not be missed. We have heard a lot of dialogue today about
how we are potentially missing opportunities. I would put it to the House that, in actual
fact, the missed opportunities all happened long before National took office in this
National-led Government.
In respect of innovation, we talked about Callaghan Innovation, but one of the
innovations that is happening inside the Tertiary Educat ion Commission and funded by
the Government is the establishment of the information and communications technology
graduation schools. These are going to be established in Auckland, Wellington, and
Christchurch. They are really good strong partnerships with  business. These will create
internships and research with high -tech firms. It is certainly that indication that we are
moving into that really connected environment —that digital environment —and as a
country, it just underlines the principle that for us to  maintain our standing in the
18556 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
OECD, as was referred to previously, every New Zealander needs the best possible
education. It is a very long continuum, but at the top end of it, the Tertiary Education
Commission has been greatly improved and refined. The ac curacy and the
accountability have been improved. We have only to look at the industry training
organisations where the Minister has focused on with legislation to add transparency,
accountability, and refinement so that we get better outcomes for those st akeholder tax-
funded activities.
But just to elaborate, one particular area that the Government will be incredibly
satisfied with is the apprenticeship reboot situation. It has moved from a provider -based
training situation, which occurred immediately aft er the Christchurch earthquakes,
where there were an amazing number of provisions for people to take up opportunities
for training, whether at the Christchurch Polytechnic Institute of Technology or with the
Southern Institute of Technology or whatever —all of those polytechs. Well, what we
are now seeing with the growth in the economy, with the growth in Auckland, with the
growth in Christchurch, and with the growth in the regions is a far greater uptake of
employer-based training. So that is your genuine apprenticeship training model, and it is
wonderful to see that we have increased that spending by $70 million. This is all very
good and it shows that we have got a very appropriately balanced Tertiary Education
Commission.

items.speaker: HONE HARAWIRA
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chairman. The
Education and Science Committee’s report on the Tertiary Education Commission made
an important point about how the Tertiary Education Commission is having t o cope
with ongoing cuts to tertiary sector funding rather than manage a stronger budget for the
sector. The sector is crying out for support at a time when we have record numbers of
young people leaving for Australia, record numbers of unemployed young pe ople, and a
refusal by the Government to properly fund tertiary education for those still living here
in Aotearoa.
That is why it is important that in considering this report on the Tertiary Education
Commission we also consider the research that tells us how the lack of access to tertiary
education defines the future for many of our young people. It is research that tells us
that high fees stop many from thinking that they can aspire to a tertiary education, from
even bothering to enrol, and from signing on for longer and more costly degree -length
courses, even though they know that that is the pathway to better employment
opportunities. It is research that tells us that many crippled by student debt leave as soon
as they graduate to escape a life of indeb tedness, or drop out early because of the heavy
financial commitments of tertiary study. Sadly enough, it is research that tells us what
most of us already know but many of us refuse to acknowledge, and that is that these
problems are ever more complex and  far more damaging for Māori, Pasifika, and for
those who grow up in communities where poverty is the norm.
That is why it is important that we say that if we want New Zealand to become a
genuine player in world affairs, then instead of trying to bribe ou r way on to the United
Nations Security Council, and instead of throwing even more money at Team New
Zealand after already blowing $90 million on two failed campaigns to date, and instead
of constantly cutting funds to what was once a leading international  tertiary sector,
perhaps we should be overhauling our whole education system and rebuilding it based
on a full commitment to free education. That would show our young people that we
want them to grow here, to learn here, to live here, to work here, and to  invest here, and
that we are happy to invest in them, because we know that an investment in them is an
investment in us all.
Of course, we know that education is a public right, and something that should be
paid for from the public purse, and that Aotear oa is a better nation with an educated
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18557
population. We know that student debt is a huge deterrent to people taking up tertiary
study and a massive burden in a low-wage economy like ours. We know that we need to
be tapping into the nation’s intelligence, to become innovators rather than mere
consumers for the world’s multinationals, and that without a culture of free education
we shall become nothing more than the zombies of the world —the dull and dimwitted
slaves to a rich, powerful, and ever greedier elite.  That is why we need to increase
access to our tertiary institutions, to convince parents that their children can get into
those places, and to get our young people to believe that tertiary education really is
available to everyone, regardless of the colour of their wallets.
That is why one of Mana’s very first policies is free education, a position also
promoted by our partners in the Internet Party, and a position based on our absolute
belief that our young people are worth every cent of our investment. That is why we say
this. Drop the decision to shut down student associations, and let them continue to be
voices for change, campaigners for student rights, and advocates for freethinking. Dump
the plan to remove students, staff, and community members from  tertiary governance
bodies, and let them continue to be the voices of their communities. Write off student
debt, as the first step in our investment in our own future, provide a proper living
student allowance for all tertiary students, scrap tertiary fee s, and challenge ourselves to
create a world that we want for all of our young people, not just those who can afford it.
Yes, we know that this approach will cost us, but in the final analysis, Mana still says
yes, and absolutely yes, because we absolutely  believe that our young people will be
worth every single cent. Kia ora tātou.
Hon STEVEN JOYCE (Minister for Tertiary Education, Skills and
Employment): I just want to make a short contribution in terms of some of the
comments made by the honourable member Hone Harawira. Firstly, it is important to
note that funding has not been cut to the tertiary education sector. In fact, the increase in
investment in public tertiary institutions since 2008 is 14 percent, and the increase in the
university sector since 2008 is 18.6 percent. It is also important for him to note that the
number of qualifications granted by the New Zealand system has been growing ve ry
strongly as a result of our focus on results. We are now up to 162,000 qualifications
achieved in the 2012 year and also significantly the highest level of qualifications at the
degree level and above, at around 25,000. The other good news, given his re ferences to
struggles for young Māori and Pasifika, is that the numbers of young Māori and Pasifika
people studying at university have gone up by around 3,000 each, from memory. That is
good news as well; it is a significant increase.
In terms of the cost  of student loans to individuals, they are currently paying them
back, if they stay in the country, in around 6 to 7 years on average. I think the member
pretty much nailed a multibillion -dollar increase in expenditure in the tertiary sector in
that short speech, including writing off student loans, a much larger student allowance,
and free tertiary education for all, so he might need to cuddle up with the Greens and
their money-printing machine, but at least it will be a 3 -D printer, and I suppose that is
positive.
The New Zealand tertiary education system is very high performing. It does a very
good job for students. It actually covers 70 percent of the cost of their tuition. It
provides student loans, which are then written off, because there is no inter est—of
around 40 percent—on student loans if you stay in the country, and of course there are
also student allowances available for many students as well. It is a very generous
student support system, given the private benefits that are obtained from terti ary
education, for example. The slight irony of Mr Harawira commenting about this is that
tertiary graduates achieve an income roughly about 50 percent of premium over those
who never go to university. The irony of making those who never go to university p ay
18558 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
for those who do seems a little bit strange. But of course, this is a contest of ideas, and
that is appropriate.
The other point that I would make in closing is that, as I say, we have a very strongly
performing tertiary sector that is delivering great  results and we are working to improve
it further, with a particular interest in some of the skilled areas like information and
communications technology, engineering, science, and agriculture, where we definitely
need more people, and that is a programme that is continuing. I think that the Tertiary
Education Commission is doing a good job. It is always a work in progress, but I think
Mr Harawira needs to go and look at some of the facts about the performance that we
are achieving in the sector. Thank you.
Report noted.
Accident Compensation Corporation

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: The Accident
Compensation Corporation is a Kiwi treasure. For 40 years now it has been providing
no-fault, no -liability compensation and treatment for people in New Zealand who are
injured. We all pay into it and we all expect it to be there for us when we need it, and
for the most part, it is. There is almost nothing like it elsewh ere in the world. It is
something that New Zealanders should be immensely proud of. But over the last 5
years, under this National Government, the faith of Kiwis in ACC has been sorely
tested. We know that it has been overcharging people on their levies. W e know that it
has been finding spurious reasons to avoid paying out compensation, to avoid providing
treatment, and that it has dramatically cut its investment across the board in preventing
injuries.
We know as well that people have lost their trust in ACC to keep their private
details—their medical details —private and available only to the people who really
ought to have them. And we know, with recent developments, that ACC has actually
been collecting far too much information. For those people who actually turned round to
ACC and said; “I’m sorry, but the law does not allow you to collect this much
information.”, we know that under National they had their compensation cut. That is
why people are losing faith in what ought to be an absolute national treasure.
But the abuse of the ACC has reached new heights this year as this Government has
struggled to prove to New Zealand that it has managed to get the books back into
surplus. That was the big goal for the 2014 -15 Budget. It was that the National
Government would get the Government books back into surplus. My goodness, it has
stretched the truth in all manner of ways to try to convince New Zealanders of that, but
the biggest travesty is what it is doing in ACC.

items.speaker: ACC came to the Government and said
items.text: “You know when you put the fees up when
you first came into Government? You know when you racked everybody’s ACC levies
up far higher than they needed to be? Well, we’ve taken enough money. We’re more
than fully funded. ” In fact, the work account has nearly 140 percent of the funding it
needs not just to meet this year’s claims but all the future costs of those claims. It has
not just the 100 percent that it needs to meet those claims but another 40 percent on top
of that. The earners account is 130 percent funded—

items.speaker: Dr David Clark
items.text: 130 percent?

items.speaker: IAIN LEES -GALLOWAY
items.text: —130 percent funded —and yet this Government
continues to overcharge Kiwis on their ACC levies. Why? Because the levies that  come
in go towards the National Government’s supposed, made -up, phoney surplus. So New
Zealanders are paying far too much on their ACC levies and $50 a year too much on
their car registration just so that the National Government can pretend that it is doi ng a
good job with the economy and that it has got the books back into surplus. Look, getting
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18559
the books back into surplus was a really positive goal for this Government to have
had—we applaud that —but it should have done it through economic growth. It shou ld
have done it by getting Kiwis back into work so that it was taking more income tax —so
that Kiwis could afford to spend money at the supermarket so they might pay more
GST. That is how the Government should have got the income up, not by charging
people far more than it needed to on its ACC levies.
And the Government is not doing it just this year; it is planning to do it next year as
well. ACC has said that it can cut levies by $650 million and the corporation would still
be sustainable. Is the Governme nt going to do that? No way. No way is it going to cut
$650 million from those ACC levies, because it still needs that money so that it can
pretend that it has got the books back into surplus.
New Zealanders love ACC. They love the fact that it is there when they need it. They
love the fact that it is more cost -effective than any other insurance scheme anywhere
else in the world. They hated the fact that the National Government was going to try to
privatise it. Thankfully, it has given up on that idea. The National Government needs to
give up on overcharging Kiwis on their ACC levies and start giving New Zealanders a
fair deal.
SIMON O’CONNOR (National —Tāmaki): I am very pleased to be here to  speak
on ACC in this debate. It is disappointing to have heard Iain Lees -Galloway, the last
speaker, being so angry and frustrated, in some ways, that the National Government has
actually put the ACC books in order and is competently able to actually star t returning
levies—[Interruption] You see, those members are yelling and screaming. They do not
like it, you see, because we know exactly the Labour record on ACC. Like a number of
things that we picked up when we came into Government, it was in bad shape and in
disorder. We know that with the claim costs. I have just got a note here, and I was
noticing that the cost of claims increased by about 57 percent in 4 years under Labour. It
has an inability to actually run ACC properly and appropriately. It is a s ort of cash cow
approach, and it has actually taken the National Government to take the bull by the
horns, tidy things up, fix things up, and not only return the books to such a state that we
are able to reduce levies in order to return money to Kiwis but to actually line up and
put a focus not only on the care that is required through ACC but also on prevention,
and to have those two line up. So I think we can be very proud of what ACC is doing.
I know that over recent weeks, actually, in the Transport an d Industrial Relations
Committee we had people from the sensitive claims unit of ACC come in and give us a
briefing. It was a really interesting insight into the work that they do. It is really
important work. As a constituent MP, I often get people coming  in on ACC issues. I
think it is important to acknowledge that it is a fraught area and, more often than not, it
actually causes difficulty for people. I suppose it is one of the roles as a member of
Parliament to try to advocate on those issues. So nothin g is perfect by any means, but
ACC is actually in good shape and in good form.
We know that in the most recent Budget we have indicated another total of $480
million worth of levy cuts for Kiwis this year and into next year—really important—and
a lot of t hat is going to actually focus on the motor vehicle account and the levies there
on motor vehicles. In fact, from next year Kiwis may well find that their registration
costs are down by about $130. Why? Once again, we have focused on allowing ACC to
do its core job and to do it well, and, therefore, to return money to Kiwis where it is due.
Unfortunately, all we have heard from the Opposition is a lot of angry vitriol that this
might be done at all. So that is really important there. The levy cuts, though, that have
been indicated in the Budget are sitting on top of a whole series of levy cuts so far. As
of 1 April this year New Zealanders started saving about $387 million in ACC levies
over the last year itself. So that has made New Zealand households about  $180 better
18560 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
off, and, actually, large employers could have saved up to $6,000 a year as well in terms
of levies. So when we look at what the Government does, it is a broad approach, and
ACC has been part of that.
But a big chunk too is not simply putting the accounts in order. It is not simply trying
to provide the best service to Kiwis but also focusing on that preventative side. We
know that ACC spends a lot of money in this area because of the old adage that
prevention is better than cure, and there has been a major reboot in the injury prevention
activities of ACC. In fact, we have seen a doubling of the investment in this space. We
have also seen, I think it is important to mention, particularly in the light of the report
released by Sir Owen Glenn ye sterday, that a big focus of ACC —and driven by this
Government—is on preventing sexual and family violence. There is a lot more work
working within the educative space to try to put these messages out. As I said at the
start, we had the sensitive claims un it come in and talk us through the work that it does.
We are also conscious of work that is happening within the integrated services for
sensitive claims. This work should go live in November this year. There is really
important work in that space.
In closing, I think one good thing to note in particular around this is the level of care
that ACC already provides for people who are seeking assistance because of sexual
abuse, domestic violence, and so forth. They can get 16 hours of immediate support
from ACC. A claim has to be lodged, but they do not have to wait for the confirmation
of that claim to get help. It is just a small example of the activities and the changes that
are occurring in this space. So, returning to where I was at the start, I think we o n this
side can be rightly proud of the focus of ACC and the work that it is doing, and proud
that we are returning money to New Zealanders and that they are not having to pay
more on their levies than they need to. Thank you.
Report noted.
Electoral Commission

items.speaker: Hon Dr PITA SHARPLES
items.text: I take a call on the
Electoral Commission, including the functions of the Chief Electoral Officer. If one was
to look at the 2012 -13 financial review that was presented to the Justice and Electoral
Committee, it would be pretty underwhelming —two sentences, in fact —with the
emphasis being that there were no matters to bring to the attention of the House. Well, I
would have thought that the fact that only 58 percent of the indigenous people of this
land turned up to vote in the last general election might have been a matter of some
concern to the Crown entity charged with promoting public awareness of electoral
matters as part of its responsibility for preparing and conducting general elections. In
stark number terms, although there are 462,000 Māori who are of voting age and are
eligible to vote, fewer than 270,000 proceeded to take up that voting opportunity at the
ballot box. Forty thousand Māori disappeared at the first hurdle —that is, the enrolment
table. But when we get to the turnout of the vote, the statistics are deplorable.
The Electoral Commission is an independent Crown entity. It should operate
strategies to increase democratic participation without being accused of a bias towards
any political party. In 2012-13 its total revenue was $27 million, but here is the irony: in
the 2012 -13 financial review the Electoral Commission spent only $22 million,
returning a surplus of close to $5 million —$5 million that could usefully have been
spent in investing in the challenge of how to increase Māori electoral turnout and, in
doing so, how to improve the effectiveness of our democracy. I would hasten to say that
the issue of low turnout is not only a feature of Māori voting preferences. In a paper by
Jack Vowles, entitled Down, Down, Down: Turnout in New Zealand from 1946 to the
2011 Election , Mr Vowles reported the views of one commentator who declared the
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18561
relative ab sence of voters in the polling booths in 2011 as “the saddest day for
democracy in New Zealand”. In fact, Mr Vowles concludes that to find a New Zealand
election with a lower official turnout than in 2011, one must go back to 1887, well
before women attained voting rights.
So I am sorry, I cannot fathom how the Justice and Electoral Committee found
nothing to report on when looking at the financial review of the Electoral Commission.
Voting is of paramount importance to the running of a healthy democracy. It is about
the people being empowered to take action, to cast a vote, and to make their voice
heard. We need to be out and proud. Casting our vote is our right, it is our duty, and it is
our responsibility. The power of voting is the power of change. It i s the power of
voicing views and of making a mark in history.
The Māori Party has a couple of ideas on how we could make the change our nation
needs so clearly in terms of voting participation. We have drafted legislation to enable
all Māori to be automatically entered on the Māori roll with an option to transfer to the
general roll, instead of the other way round. This would take the complexity out of the
Māori electoral option campaign, given that the majority of Māori are enrolled on the
Māori roll. It would make sense to make that roll the default roll and give ot her
individuals a choice to opt out on to the general roll if they see fit. Another key
campaign that the Māori Party recommends is encouraging a focus on education for
engaged and active citizenship. We need to increase the ease of voting, make voting
more exciting, increase its relevance, and make it easier to register to vote.
Last week I introduced a new curriculum priority in ensuring Māori history is
known, taught, and promoted in our schools. I am hopeful that with new emphasis on
knowing our storie s, it may well encourage a far stronger reason why all New
Zealanders understand the value of the vote and the significance of having a say.
Representation in a democracy is not only a basic human right but it is also necessary if
we want to make sure our nation moves forward together. I hope that the next time the
Electoral Commission comes up for debate before the Committee there will indeed be
something to talk about —a new energy and a commitment to making our voices heard.
Thank you.
Report noted.
New Zealand Railways Corporation
DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First) : The performance of KiwiRail management has
been so poor that it should be fired. This is a company that has spent mega -millions of
public mon ey with very little to show for it, and this Government has sat back and
twiddled its thumbs while things get worse and worse. The Government has seen to it
that the New Zealand Railways Corporation gets far too little resources to improve its
network. In Auckland the expansion of the city rail network will be far too slow while
the Government instead spends more and more billions of dollars on a motorway
expansion programme that cannot solve that region’s transport problems.
In the Hawke’s Bay the mothballed Napier to Gisborne line has not been repaired for
the paltry $4 million required for that purpose, despite the Prime Minister’s original
statement soon after the slips closing the line occurred that the road would never be
enough by itself. The slips that closed the line are one thing, but now the slippage by the
Government in failing to repair that line is completely another. That is totally
unacceptable not only to New Zealand First but also to the majority of people in that
region, and for good reaso n. Since those slips occurred that closed that line, $4
million—about the same that would be required to repair the line —has been spent on
the Gisborne to Napier road, on just a few passing lanes. So the Government can find
money for that, but it cannot find money to keep the line open.
18562 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
But the elephant in the room —or should I say the ship —is the KiwiRail Cook Strait
services. Anyone can see that this comedy of errors shows serious mismanagement of
this service by an incompetent management and board. We ha ve seen breakdowns and
mishaps one after the other in that service, resulting from what is best called a floating
lemon, the Aratere. Then, of course, it was lengthened, and as soon as a laden train was
put on it, it showed a tendency to flex because the l engthening of that ship was not
appropriate for the vessel. Then a series of mishaps followed. Here is a list of just a few
of them: the ship bending along the keel and twisting when under load, toilets not
working properly, problems with lifeboats, the freight capacity for trucks being reduced,
the ship breaking down within a few days of arriving back into service, the engines not
being powerful enough to drive the ship through heavy seas because of the extra weight
and length, and an infestation of rats. It has had problems with the cargo doors,
stabiliser, ballast, and radar, and, of course, with a propeller falling off. And then there
are the thousands of litres of fuel that were lost somewhere—a litany of errors, as I have
said.
This company simply doe s not know what it is doing. KiwiRail’s Cook Strait ferry
operation is a chapter of errors and of sheer incompetence and dangerous blunders, and
the Aratere is now on its way back from Singapore. Let us hope it makes it. What has
been the true cost of the ferry? Is it $100 million dollars, $150 million, or $200 million?
It is hard to tell. So it is not just a lemon; it is a longer lemon, but not only that, it is a
very expensive lemon too. When it gets back, it will still have restrictions on freight and
sailing conditions, so it is not just a lemon but a limited lemon as well —all because
KiwiRail’s management could not get it right.
Now we understand that the company is seriously thinking about buying the Stena
Alegra—another lemon, a cast -off from another  country, and not suited to Cook Strait
conditions at all. And the price, we understand, is $8 million —a cheap, nasty rust
bucket, even more prone to breakdowns than the Aratere. This boat uses 20 times the
lubricant of other ferries. Why would that be? We  all know that a car that is burning oil
has a serious engine problem. This rust bucket is at the end of its useful life.
Report noted.
Solid Energy New Zealand

items.speaker: CATHERINE DELAHUNTY
items.text: Solid Energy is not a solid story; it is a sad
story, especially when we know that our environment is our economy. We do need our
State-owned enterprises to be solid and no one could describe what has happened to
Solid Energy in the last financial term of  Parliament as being solid at all. It is a sad
story, from the failed lignite project through to the recent 170 redundancies at the
Stockton mine, which is costing families dearly. Solid Energy is in a slump for two
reasons: one is mismanagement, and the o ther is that the coal industry globally is in a
serious slump. Solid Energy has been badly managed and is wrecking the environment,
without any employment security for the people of the West Coast. Even coking coal is
not holding up as the Chinese steel in dustry also slows down. We have only to talk to
Australia about the state of the coal industry as the basis for your economy to know that
it is not a stable basis for a good economy.
But, as George Monbiot said this week: “An ounce of hope is worth a ton of
despair.” There is perhaps not a lot of hope associated with Solid Energy’s current
performance and its reliance on fossil fuels. Many people, including the Greens,
recognise that coal is the past and it kills the climate, and that clean energy and look ing
after the environment is our only viable future. We have a beautiful country. We have
relied on coal in the past, and what we have seen is that the global coal price and
environmental damage shows this State -owned asset is in a bad way. I attended the
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18563
Education and Science Committee when Solid Energy came and spoke about the state
of its books, and it denied it was thinking of trying to get overseas buyers to take over,
including some of the Indian State coal people.
But whatever is its future, its pre sent is very shaky, and no one will deny that. Solid
Energy, like all of us, needs to build a future that is based on clean energy, renewables,
and meaningful sustainability. It cannot keep trying to relive the past. If we do what we
have always done, we will get what we have always gotten, and that is a boom -and-bust
economy for the mining towns, including Huntly and on the West Coast, where despite
many years of coal extraction there is still severe poverty in those communities. I have
driven through thos e communities and seen the homes. If coal was ever going to
deliver, it would have. Instead, coal has damaged the environment permanently —and
Stockton is a dreadful sight —but it has not created the sustainable work that the people
deserve. No community should be at the mercy of an international price that can destroy
and make the difference between employment and survival or despair.
We are for a positive and hopeful view of what companies like Solid Energy could
be, but in order for them to be that, we ne ed change. In a progressive Government the
Greens would oppose new coalmines. We are proud to say that we have launched a
climate policy that would make polluters like coalminers pay, and our climate policy
has been well -received. As people would have hear d at question time when Russel
Norman talked about it, there are many commentators from all sides of the political
spectrum who do not believe that coal is the future, do not believe that fossil fuels can
be managed the way they have been managed, do not s upport emissions trading
schemes—because they are “clip the ticket” failures —and do support the positive
moves that we have made for a transition to a just economy based on a sustainable
climate.
There is much hope to be had in protecting and valuing our environment. It is a very
tough call for coal communities. We can have no illusions about the price of transition,
but we here in this House have a responsibility to the future and to those communities,
and we have to build that transition. We can do that.  We can innovate. We can set up a
Green Investment Bank. We can protect the climate through sensible and fair climate
policies that do not hurt people. We can support Solid Energy to change. We can say to
Solid Energy that we will support a real, genuine investment in those things. We can say
to those communities that regional development is a real thing. The Government has a
role to play as a partner in supporting the parts of the country that have been dependent
on companies like Solid Energy, which canno t deliver to them reliable jobs in a clean
environment for the future. I am under no illusion how tough that call is. This is not said
lightly. This is not said with disrespect to the people who have lost their jobs. I come
from a community that was once d ependent on mining, and we have built our way out
of it. We are fortunate to have done that, because we can survive on ecotourism. We can
survive on—
Report noted.
Bay of Plenty District Health Board

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It gives me great pleasure to stand and
talk about the wonderful job that the Bay of Plenty District Health Board has done. If
you look at the statistics, I think they speak for themselves and they dese rve to be heard
in this House. First of all, can I congratulate the Minister of Health, because he has
overseen a funding increase to this district health board over the last 5 years of an extra
$127 million.

items.speaker: Dr Cam Calder
items.text: How much?
18564 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: It is $127 million extra to the Bay of Plenty District Health
Board. That has then enabled that health board to deliver some of the most amazing
results. We have seen that it has employed more staff. We have had 67 more doctors
and 132 more nurses employed by this district health board —again, over the last 5
years. More important than even the staff, and in any district health board I do not want
to underestimate the effect and the work that the staff do, but actually health car e is all
about patients. What we have seen through the extra funding and the extra staff is that
over 11,000 more patients have been treated for electives than were treated under
Labour. That is an increase of 11,215 more patients treated than were treated  under the
Labour Government—over 11,000. The particular one that affects many, many people,
particularly in my electorate, is orthopaedic surgery, and we have seen a 52 percent
increase in orthopaedic surgeries carried out by the Bay of Plenty District He alth Board.
That is people’s hips, knees, and all the other bits and pieces that they have replaced,
and I think that that is something to thank all those staff working in the health board for.
They have delivered it across quite a big area. It goes right up to the tip of the East
Cape, so they are large rural areas.
The most exciting event I think in the last year was the opening by the Minister of
Health last week of the rebuilt Whakatāne Hospital, and $67 million was contributed by
this National -led Gov ernment to rebuild the Whakatāne Hospital. A great deal of
planning and hard work went into that. It is quite interesting that when I became the MP
for the East Coast electorate, there was a lot of talk around what was going to happen to
the Whakatāne Hosp ital. It had severe asbestos and seismic problems, and under the
previous Labour Government consultation meetings were held, and all sorts were talked
about the replacement of the Whakatāne Hospital. But when we came into Government,
when National came int o Government, what do you think we found? There had been a
lot of talk but actually the money cupboard was bare. There was no money allocated. In
fact, despite all the community consultation and all the discussions that the health board
had had with the co mmunity, the Whakatāne Hospital was not even on the list for
capital improvements.
I went to work and, fortunately, the Minister of Health was sympathetic, because this
Whakatāne area serves an enormous rural area. It is an area that takes in many, many
small communities that are very low in the social deprivation scales. People have severe
transport difficulties but they also have severe health issues. The thought of having to
go from the tip of the East Cape to Tauranga Hospital was just ridiculous. The health
care of the people of that Eastern Bay of Plenty area would have severely suffered if this
National Government had not stepped in and spent $67 million on rebuilding the
Whakatāne Hospital. To the Minister of Health I want to say I know that my
constituents are exceedingly grateful for the work that this John Key - led National
Government has done, because we put our money where our mouth is. We did not just
talk about it; we got out there and we rebuilt it. The hospital had an open day that
attracted over 2,000 people to come and have a look through the rebuilt hospital, and
last week Minister Ryall and I officially opened the hospital. That means our region has
high-quality health care.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I would like to associate myself with the
comments of the MP for the East Coast, Anne Tolley, on this financial review of the
Bay of Plenty District Health Board. Health boards in New Zealand can pretty much be
divided into three groups. One is a group that has fast -growing populations, another has
very stable populations, and a third group has depopulations. Each of those groups
presents significant challenges.
The most significant challenge or strategic issue th at the Bay of Plenty District
Health Board has faced is actually keeping up with a rapidly growing population and
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18565
also a growing older population. That is why the district health board, together with the
almost $130 million of extra funding that our Govern ment has given, has been able to
invest in significant numbers of extra doctors, significant numbers of extra nurses, and,
I think, a 52 percent increase in hips, knees, and other orthopaedic procedures to reflect
the ageing population. But, at the same ti me, it has not only dealt with that fast -growing
population in the west —and there have been significant investments in the new east
wing at the Tauranga Hospital and the purchase of the RSA land, which is now the
clinical school, so there have been big inv estments there in the west —there has also
been a need to invest in the east, which is a predominantly lower -income community. It
has a much higher Māori population than the west. So there are a whole lot of issues
that have happened there.
Our Government has not only been investing very strongly in primary care. You
cannot have strong primary-care developments in isolation from good hospital services.
That is the reason why, with the very strong advocacy of the MP for the East Coast, Mrs
Anne Tolley, the Government has put $67 million into a new state -of-the-art hospital in
Whakatāne. It is a tremendous investment. I had the opportunity to tour the facilities
there on Friday. It is fantastic how well that facility integrates with the primary care
services in that community. It is very important for the Bay of Plenty.
But what makes it more exciting is that the people at the Bay of Plenty District
Health Board are recognising that health care changes. Mrs Tolley talked about the
people who live way up at the  top of the cape. Transport issues are very significant in
the Bay of Plenty because of the isolation of the people of Te Whānau -a-Apanui and
also of the people of Ngāti Manawa in the Murupara area. There are also issues around
Kawerau, where there are a lot of low-income people. The Bay of Plenty District Health
Board is actually at the forefront of telehealth in New Zealand. A significant investment
has gone into providing telehealth. By way of example, in Ōpōtiki, up the coast, and in
Kawerau and Murupara, patients can go into their general practitioner’s clinic and have
an online Skype -type conversation —but higher quality than Skype —with a specialist
either from Whakatāne Hospital or from Tauranga Hospital. You can see the significant
benefits that they have.
Similarly, in Ōpōtiki the rest homes are now linked in too. So there was a patient
who was a resident in a rest home who had a turn. They were able to use the telehealth
Skype-based technology for the general practitioner to be in his home and consu lting
with the rest home resident in her home over the telecommunication network, and
similarly with patients up the coast. We are investing very strongly not only in the
bricks and mortar but also in the new technology that allows people to have much fast er
and more convenient access to all this expertise around the health service.
Similarly, the Bay of Plenty District Health Board has entered into a public -private
partnership with the development of private radiotherapy services that will be available
there from the end of September. This is a very significant investment. What it means is
that cancer patients in the Bay of Plenty who would previously have had to travel to
Hamilton for their radiotherapy will be able to receive that treatment at private fa cilities
integrated into Tauranga Hospital. That is really the next big step in services for people
of the Bay of Plenty —this really significant investment that has been made by private
investors, who will be able to treat not only private patients but als o public patients, and
there will be the opportunity over time to have neighbouring district health board
patients treated there, as well. There are very, very good public hospital cancer services
in the oncology area there, but this radiation treatment wi ll provide just that extra suite
of services to benefit patients. It is a pretty smart public -private partnership that enjoys
the support of the wider population in that area.
18566 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014
So I just acknowledge the tremendous work of the people of the Bay of Plenty
District Health Board. With my 24 years as a member of Parliament, I can say that I
think the service being provided is sterling. There is a real dedication and commitment
there, and I think we can be very proud of the clinicians there.
Report noted.
Southern District Health Board

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I am very pleased for the people of
Whakatāne that they have now got a new hospital. Some may recall that there was a
march and a “hands around the hospital” event in 1999 because the then National
Government looked to close it. I think it is really important that you do put your money
where your mouth is when it comes to building hospitals. I would like to say that when
in Government we rebuilt Kaitāia; that was to be closed. We rebuilt Thames; that was to
be closed. We rebuilt the new Auckland Hospital and the new Wellington Regional
Hospital. We did work on Waikato Hospital. We rebuilt the Wairarapa Hospital. The
Wairau Hospi tal in Blenheim, the Invercargill hospital, the Dunstan Hospital, the
refurbishment of the Timaru Hospital, the Christchurch Women’s Hospital, Murchison,
Nelson—this was under a Labour Government. So when we get the great applause from
members over there f or their wonderful work, it would be nice if sometimes they
recognised that there was a lot of capital work that went on under Labour. Many of
those hospitals were in threat of closure under a National Government.
I want to talk about the Southern District Health Board. I am glad that the Minister of
Health is in the chair, because he has been incredibly evasive and elusive of late. He has
not been to a single political forum in the last 18 months, so it would be nice to actually
have him in front of a rea l crowd where he could be questioned —like the doctors on
Friday, when he failed to turn up. But the people of Dunedin, the people of the south,
have been, I believe, neglected by this Government. Six years on, this is the worst
hospital in terms of need of  improvement in New Zealand. We hear about how big the
geographic area is in the Bay of Plenty, but the biggest geographic area trying to
provide health services is the Otago-Southland area.

items.speaker: All the Minister has answered with is
items.text: “Oh, you didn’t do anythi ng when you were
Minister.” Well, I have to say, Minister, you were told that this hospital was leaking. I
asked you a question, Minister, about the leaking of this hospital and you gave me an
answer claiming that there had been one leak in this hospital. I have the answer. It is to
written question No. 1699. You said there had been one leak, a one -off leak,
experienced in 2012 in this hospital. That was your knowledge, Minister, of this
hospital. In fact, there had been many leaks in this hospital. There w ere leaks in
theatres—leaking into the electrical cords in the theatre. They said about this leak:
“Urgent, please come and fix it. Water is dripping through the light fittings in theatre 4.
This is urgent. We are undergoing an operation.” There have been leaks dripping
through the corridor windows. The Minister overlooked the fact that there had been
numerous leaks in this hospital in the operating theatre, on their sterile equipment. He
said there had been one. When asked if he would help provide some mon ey to fix the
leaks, he said, no, he did not intend to give them any money. He said: “I’ve given them
$124 million since we became the Government.”
So why should the people of Otago have to put up with theatres that are dripping and
leaking, and he will p rovide no assistance in terms of fixing them? In fact, the district
health board has estimated that the rebuild of this hospital is 7 years away —7 years.
That will make it 13 years if National is still in Government.
Then, if that was not bad enough, the district health board has such a poor IT system
that it lost 3,000 mammograms. Three thousand mammograms were lost as a result of
17 Jun 2014 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 18567
IT failure in the Southern District Health Board. That is a travesty. So many women
were worried about what had happened to th em and there was a very, very poor
response from the board. I would have thought that the Minister would step in at that
point and ask for the report on the IT failure to be released. That report has not been
released to the public of Otago, and, like many  things in that area, it has been covered
up. So I would like the Minister, when he takes his call, in his skite sheet to tell us about
the colonoscopy problem down there and tell us the truth about the number of
colonoscopies that have not been done in that region.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I would like to thank that member,
Annette King, for her reminiscences from last century. It is so nice to hear about what
she was doing wh en she was Minister of Health last century. She spent all this money
when there was more money than the Government knew what to do with, and she never
did a thing for Dunedin Hospital. All she and her cronies ever did for 9 years was mine
the asset, replace nothing, do no maintenance, and run the facilities down. It was so bad
that in her last year as Minister of Health she was berating her own Labour appointees
for running deficits of over $9 million for years on end. So when the money was raining
out of t he sky, how much money did Annette King give to Dunedin Hospital to fix its
buildings? Nothing. She just mined the asset and did nothing. But wait for it —the
Budget went up, and did it get money for buildings? No.
But look at her record on operations for the people of the south. In her first year as
Minister of Health 8,800 people got elective surgery —8,800. When she left office,
8,400 had got elective surgery, so fewer people got elective surgery when she finished
being Minister of Health than when she st arted being Minister of Health. When Annette
King left as Minister of Health, 8,400 operations were done that year at Dunedin
Hospital. This last year under review there were 10,270 elective operations. She left
with 8,400; today, it is 10,270, in 2012 -13. She had 6 years and fewer people got
operations. I have had 6 years and we have increased the number massively from when
she was Minister of Health. We have put an extra $124 million in there, 82 more
doctors, 116 more nurses, and an emergency department that Dunedin can be proud of
because there are not people lying around the corridors unsafe for hours and hours and
hours, which I inherited.

items.speaker: Hon Michael Woodhouse
items.text: What happened to the neonatal unit?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: Oh, the neonatal unit —shameful! The neonatal unit —
shameful! This was for the most vulnerable babies born at Dunedin Hospital, stuck into
the smallest footprint you could possibly find. It was not a good service. In 9 years of a
Labour Government nothing happened, and we put the money in and our Prime
Minister was there opening a state -of-the-art neonatal intensive care unit at Dunedin
Hospital, an investment by this Government when the money was tight. When the
money was tight we found the money to put in a new neonatal intensive care unit.
I have to say that I get fantastic feedback from Dunedin for the investment that our
Government has made in that neonatal intensive care unit. I get amazing feedback from
Dunedin on the massive improvements at the emergency department. People in Dunedin
now know—

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Tell us about the colonoscopies.

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: I will tell you about the colonoscopies. Under Labour, people
who had a family history of colorectal cancer w ere denied the ability to go and have a
surveillance colonoscopy. Labour stopped surveillance colonoscopy at Dunedin;
National has started it again. Labour stopped surveillance colonoscopy; we have started
it.

items.speaker: Hon Annette King
items.text: Where?
18568 Debate on Crown Entities etc. 17 Jun 2014

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: We have started it at Dunedin. So that is the truth of that
member’s failure.
I am not going to harp on about last century, because it is so different now from
when that member came in in 1984. The Dunedin Hospital is a much better place. The
services are improving. More patients are getting elective surgery. Remember that
between 1999 and 2005 fewer patients got elective surgery —fewer patients got elective
surgery—and now under our Government record numbers of patients are ge tting
elective surgery at Dunedin Hospital, the emergency department is working better, the
cancer services are fantastic and working faster, and we are getting more preventive
care for the children of the Otago -Southland region. Right across the board thi s district
health board is delivering on service and this Government is giving it the money and the
staff to improve care for people in Dunedin.

items.speaker: Hon ANNETTE KING
items.text: I wis h to table an Official
Information Act request on the number of leaks at Dunedin Hospital—

items.speaker: The CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Leave is sought for that purpose. Is there
any objection? There is no objection. It can be tabled.
